01-001.json.summary: After opening prayers, the great sages visit King Shatanika, who honours them and asks to hear a teaching of duty. Vyasa sends him to his pupil Sumantu. The sages praise the Bharata and the books of duty. Sumantu names the law-givers and the eighteen Puranas, and Shatanika asks for the Bhavishya, which he has not yet heard. Sumantu lists what it will cover: conduct, rites of life, marriage, kingship, holy places, vows and gods. He also gives who it was passed down through, from Brahma to Sumantu, and the rewards of hearing it.

01-002.json.summary: Sumantu tells Shatanika that this Purana has five parts and five marks, including creation, secondary creation and lineages, and he lists the fourteen and eighteen branches of learning. He then describes creation: the dark unmanifest world, the golden egg, Brahma, the elements, the first sages, the beings of all kinds and the four classes with their duties. He explains the divisions of time, from a blink of the eye to a day of Brahma, and the four ages with their changing duties and lifespans. The chapter ends with the forty rites of a Brahmin, the eight inner qualities, and the rewards of hearing it.

01-003.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the birth rites and the duties of the stages of life. Sumantu lists the early rites: the birth rite, naming, first feeding, tonsure and initiation, with their usual ages and the class-wise rules for names, girdles, threads and staffs. He gives rules for begging and eating, and tells the story of the merchant Dhanavardhana, who broke his meal and died. He then explains rinsing the mouth with water for purity, the sacred places on the hand and the gods pleased by touching each part of the body.

01-004.json.summary: Sumantu continues to Shatanika with the rules for a Brahmin student after initiation. He gives the ages for the hair-cutting rite (sixteen for a Brahmin, twenty-two for a Kshatriya, twenty-four for a Vaishya) and says women's tonsure is done without mantras. The teacher teaches cleanliness, conduct, the fire rite and the twilight prayers, and the student keeps his hands joined and the senses controlled. The chapter explains Om, the three great calls and the Savitri (Gayatri), says reciting is better than other sacrifices, and says one who neglects the twilights is treated like a Shudra. It gives rules for greeting, for the five kinds of teacher, and for who should be taught and who should not. It lists what a student must avoid, such as honey, meat, perfumes, gambling, lies and slander, and how he lives by alms, serves the teacher and behaves toward the teacher's wife and family. It says mother, father and teacher are the three fires and the three worlds. It allows learning from a lower person in need, and ends by naming the best seasons for initiation: spring for a Brahmin, summer for a Kshatriya and autumn for a Vaishya.

01-005.json.summary: Sumantu says a student may study three Vedas for thirty-six years, or less, and then, with his teacher's leave, take a wife of his own class who has good marks. Shatanika asks for the marks of women, and Sumantu repeats what Brahma told the sages, going over the body from the feet up: feet, toes, nails, ankles, legs, knees, thighs, waist, belly, back, breasts, arms, neck, jaw, lips, tongue, teeth, nose, eyebrows, eyes, ears, forehead, hair and voice and gait, and saying which signs bring wealth, children and happiness and which bring poverty, widowhood or trouble. It adds which girls not to marry (for example by tawny colour, disease, or names of stars, trees, rivers or fearful things) and ten kinds of families to avoid. It closes by saying that good conduct counts more than the marks, and that one who marries a girl with such marks gains prosperity and fame.

01-006.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the good conduct of women. Sumantu repeats what Brahma said after giving the marks of women. A householder should first win wealth, since a poor man's house is a trouble, and seeing a wife and children hungry is worse than hell. Wealth is the root of duty, desire and the other aims, and a man without a wife or without money has no right to them. A man is only half a man until he has a wife, so he should marry at the right time, a girl of a suitable family. The chapter then describes three kinds of marriage ties, with families lower, equal or higher. Ties among equals are best, and ties with higher or lower families bring shame. It ends by saying a close tie is one that shows in shared dishes, in hard times and good, and that marriages should be made with equals.

01-007.json.summary: Brahma tells the sages about choosing a wife: she should not be of the mother's close line or the father's clan, and the first wife of a Brahmin, Kshatriya and Vaishya should be of his own class, with other wives allowed by desire. It warns that twice-born men who marry a low-born woman bring their families down, and gives examples such as Atri, Utathya, Shaunaka and others. Brahma lists the eight forms of marriage (Brahma, Daiva, Arsha, Prajapatya, Asura, Gandharva, Rakshasa and Pishacha), says which suit which class, and describes each in a line. He says the first four give sons of spiritual brilliance and the others give cruel sons. He says a father should take no price for his daughter, and that the Arsha gift of a cow and bull is not a sale. He ends by naming the lands where duty is best kept: Brahmavarta, the land of the sages, the middle country, and Aryavarta.

01-008.json.summary: Brahma tells the duties of a householder. He should do the home rites with the marriage fire, live in a good place among dutiful neighbours, and arrange his house with its parts and servants. He says women must be guarded, because lack of care causes many faults, and warns against giving them freedom, too much trust or idle company, and lists things that spoil a wife, such as bad company, wandering, idle talk and drinking. A husband with several wives should treat them equally in dress, gifts and attention, and should visit each at her proper season. Children by each should be treated alike. He tells the husband to watch the wives' feelings through trusted servants and gives examples of kings killed by their wives: Shubhadhvaja, Sauvira, Bhadrasena, Karusha, and two Kashi kings. He says a wife is half the husband's body, and that the one who follows this conduct gains the three aims of life.

01-009.json.summary: Brahma speaks briefly on the duty of women and the use of the scriptures. He says that people differ in their actions and that rules and custom must be known. He says that women have no right to study the scriptures, yet may act under their guidance, and that rules of conduct vary even among those who know the Veda. The chapter closes by saying that the root of the householder's duty is a wife devoted to her husband.

01-010.json.summary: Brahma continues on the conduct of women toward their husbands and relatives. He names three kinds of women (a maiden, a remarried woman and a courtesan) and says each may be dear, middling or disliked. A wife's conduct is outer, toward other people, and inner, toward the husband, and it should follow the husband's wishes. He lists the people she must honour: mother, father, sister, brother, uncles, the teacher, the husband's mother and aunt, nurses, elder women, and the first wife and co-wives. He warns against joking and being alone with brothers-in-law and the husband's friends, against idle company, standing at the door, looking at the road, loud laughter, and company with ascetics, bad women and fortune-tellers. He ends by saying a woman who avoids these keeps her family's name clean.

01-011.json.summary: Brahma describes how a wife should run the home. She should treat the husband's friends and enemies as he does, help in his worship and daily needs, and keep the house clean with worship at the three times of day. The chapter lists the many things she must look after: cowsheds, servants, vegetables and herbs, household tools, spices and salt, fuel and stored grain, so that nothing is lacking when it is needed.

01-012.json.summary: Brahma continues with the wife's management of the household. He gives measures for how much different grains, pulses and oil-seeds lose or gain in cooking, grinding and pressing, and how much oil, milk and ghee to expect. The wife should have thread spun from cotton, silk and wool by women who are disabled or widowed, pay servants fairly for coarse and fine work, and look after bedding, clothes and what is kept for guests and elders. She should not wear things worn by her husband's brothers. Leftover food goes to the cattle, and the chapter gives rules for milking, calves, herds and herdsmen, goats and sheep, and wages for farm workers. It teaches saving grain and spending in measure, saying the home rests on women and the household on grain. It ends by saying a wife who is capable, fortunate and diligent wins her husband over.

01-013.json.summary: Brahma describes a wife's daily duty from the time her husband wakes. She does the needed morning tasks, serves him with care and respect, and looks after the sick and those in need. He says the husband is a woman's god and describes how she should please him and her co-wives and the relatives. The chapter closes by saying that a woman who has pleased both the world and her husband is rightly praised.

01-014.json.summary: Brahma continues on a wife's conduct when her husband is away and when the household has more than one wife. While he is away she wears only simple auspicious ornaments, keeps vows and fasts, asks after news, consults astrologers, prays to the gods for his safe return, and does not go to relatives' houses without leave. When he comes back, she greets him with proper preparation. She treats the younger co-wife as a sister and the elder as a mother and their children as her own. She does not befriend those he dislikes, spends his gifts wisely, and avoids jealousy. On her turn she serves him with care, and on the other nights she goes to the elder wife with respect. The elder wife, for her part, should keep her husband's regard and be gracious. The chapter ends by saying a wife who follows this serves her husband, honours her elders, looks after servants and gains happiness here and in the next world.

01-015.json.summary: Brahma continues with advice to wives on serving a husband and keeping harmony in the home, including how to care for his body and comfort. He speaks of watching what pleases the husband, sharing household work, and bringing even a stranger to affection by kindness. The chapter ends with the usual line that a woman who follows this conduct prospers.

01-016.json.summary: Sumantu says Brahma finished the marks and conduct of women and went to his own home. He then gives the duties of a householder. The home rites are done with the marriage fire. A householder commits five small sins through the grinding stone, the mortar, the hearth, the water pot and the broom, and removes them by the five daily great sacrifices (study, offering to ancestors, fire offering, offering to beings and honouring guests). Shatanika asks what those without a fire in the house should do, and Sumantu says fasts, vows and gifts please the gods, especially fasting on lunar days. He gives what to eat each day of the fortnight (milk on the first, no salt on the second, sesame on the third, and so on to rice-barley food on the new moon), with the rewards. He tells how Brahma made the first lunar day after he made heaven and earth from the egg, how to take the vow on it with a milk meal and honouring Brahmins, and the rewards, including a flying chariot. Vishvamitra, desiring to be a Brahmin, gained Brahmin-hood in that body by keeping the lunar-day fasts, and kings of foreign peoples also kept them for this wish.

01-017.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the worship of Brahma. Sumantu describes setting up an image of Brahma with care, bathing it with fragrant water, and decorating it with garlands, canopies, flowers and incense. He lists gifts, such as cows given to a Veda scholar, and the rewards in heaven for the worshipper and his family. He ends with worship using the Gayatri and a list of the Vedic branches of learning.

01-018.json.summary: Sumantu describes a fast on the full-moon day of the month of Kartika and the chariot festival of the god, in which the four-faced Brahma is placed in a chariot and drawn by Brahmins, with a night vigil and music. He gives a rule against a Shudra drawing the chariot. He also tells of lamp-lighting on the new-moon night, the day after it, the holy first day of Chaitra, and the great merit of bathing and giving in Kartika.

01-019.json.summary: Sumantu begins the second lunar day, ruled by the Ashvins, and tells the story of King Sharyati and the sage Chyavana. Chyavana marries the king's daughter. The Ashvin twins see her and test her faithfulness. They give the old sage a young and handsome body in return for a share of the Soma offering. The sage keeps his promise, and the Ashvins give a heavenly flying chariot. The chapter ends with the merit of keeping a fast on that day.

01-020.json.summary: Shatanika asks for the vow of the second day that keeps husband and wife from being parted. Sumantu names it Ashunyashayana ("the bed that is never empty"), kept on the second day of the dark fortnight in Shravana, when Krishna lies down with Shri. After bathing and bowing to Vishnu with Lakshmi, one says a prayer asking that the home, cattle, people and the marriage not be lost, and that the bed be never empty as Vishnu's is not. One eats at night in silence and gives a fee to a Brahmin on the second day. Shatanika asks which fruits to offer, and Sumantu says sweet seasonal fruits, such as dates and citron, to be given in the bed for four months, and not bitter or sharp ones. The reward is that for three births the home is not broken and a woman does not become a widow. Shatanika asks how Janardana is honoured on a day given to the Ashvins, and Sumantu says Vishnu gave this day to the Ashvins, so both are honoured.

01-021.json.summary: Sumantu explains the third lunar day, which belongs to Gauri. A faithful wife who serves her husband is granted beauty and good fortune by Gauri. He describes a vow before Dharmaraja in which a golden image of Gauri is set up and worshipped with fragrances and ornaments, and foods and salt are given. Indrani and Rohini are named as keeping this vow. He says that Gauri is pleased with gifts of jaggery and that the vow is also kept in Bhadrapada, Magha and Vaishakha.

01-022.json.summary: Sumantu describes the vow of the fourth lunar day, a fast with a meal of sesame rice, which pleases Vinayaka and gives success. Shatanika asks why Vinayaka is the obstacle-maker, and Sumantu tells the story. Vinayaka put an obstacle in the way of Kartikeya's making of the marks (lakshana) of men and women, and the angry Kartikeya pulled out Vinayaka's tusk to kill him. Shiva stopped him and asked the reason. Kartikeya says Shiva's own mark is the skull in his hand, which is why he is called Kapali, and he threw the marks into the sea. At a gathering of gods, Brahma and Rudra argued over who is the elder, and Rudra cut off Brahma's fifth head with his nail. With the head in his hand he came to Hari, who was doing austerity on Meru. Two men born of the anger, one in white earrings and one in red, fight like Mars and Ketu at the end of an age, and a voice from the sky says they will be born on earth with Vishnu to lift the earth's burden. Vishnu gives one to the sun and one to Indra. Brahma tells Rudra to take up the skull-bearing vow, which will have its descent on earth. The ocean is called, and told to give back the marks and the tusk, and Vinayaka is given the tusk. The tale ends with the reward of hearing it: all works are done without obstacle.

01-023.json.summary: Shatanika asks how Bhima's son (Vinayaka) became lord of the Pramathas and master of obstacles. Sumantu says that in the first Krita age, seeing people prospering without hindrance and proud, Brahma set Vinayaka over obstacles and leader of the hosts. He lists the signs of someone seized by Vinayaka: dreaming of entering water, seeing shaven men or people in saffron, riding with outcastes, donkeys and camels, working without result, and not gaining a kingdom, a husband, a child, a teacher's post or profit. The remedy is a bath on the fourth day of the bright fortnight, with mustard paste, herbs and perfumes, water from several holy sources poured from four pots, mantras for good fortune, and fire offerings in the sacrificer's name. An offering is put at the crossroads with rice, sesame, fish, meat, flowers and sweets. He then worships Ambika, Vinayaka's mother, and asks for beauty, fame, sons and wealth, and feeds Brahmins. The one who does this gains success and good fortune.

01-024.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the marks of men and women. Sumantu says Guha (Kartikeya) first told them to Shiva, and then Brahma's teaching is given. One should first judge a person's lifespan, then the marks. The chapter describes the feet, soles, toes, nails, calves and knees, and says what each kind indicates, such as wealth, poverty, long travel or early death. It also mentions gaits compared to a swan, a dog, a camel and a donkey.

01-025.json.summary: Brahma goes on with the marks of men. He describes the body, from the ankles and the build of the belly and chest to the lines on the palm, and says what each sign foretells, such as long or short life, wealth, or a good or bad end. Signs like a scale, an altar, a banner or a conch on the palm are listed as good marks.

01-026.json.summary: Brahma continues with the marks of the body. He treats the hands and palms, the lips, the teeth, the voice, the eyes and the forehead lines, and says what each shows about wealth, rank, children and the manner of death. A red lip, bright teeth and a deep voice like thunder are marks of a fortunate man; some marks of the eyes are called middling. The chapter closes with the hair and the shape of the head.

01-027.json.summary: Kartikeya, in answer, gives a short account of the marks of a king. He lists the parts of the body that should be short, red or broad, and describes the skin, nails, hair and teeth, the king's sneeze and laugh, the eyes and the head. Some features are said to bring wealth and happiness, others a short life. He finishes by saying he has told the good and bad marks of men.

01-028.json.summary: Brahma now describes the marks of women. One should examine the hands, feet, fingers and nails, and the lines on the neck and the eyes. He says which marks promise a happy, faithful life with a husband and which bring harm, including the whorls on the back and navel, the feet and the breasts. Women who are unclean in conduct and lose their beauty are called frightening. Sumantu closes by saying that Brahma, having spoken, went to his own abode.

01-029.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the god of the syllable "ga", Ganesha. Sumantu describes him as four-armed, three-eyed and covered with ornaments, and gives the way to worship him with incense, sweets and mantras, with the parts of the body touched by the syllables. He then lists many mantras and rites for different aims, including turning people away and gaining protection, using Gorochana and other items.

01-030.json.summary: Sumantu gives short rites to Ganapati. An image the size of a finger joint is made of neem wood or white oleander and worshipped with incense, sesame paste, curds and ghee, and it is said to bring success in disputes at the king's door. The chapter lists the syllable mantras for head, crest, heart, mouth and eyes, and eight hand-signs. A worshipper who fasts on the fourth lunar day and keeps this rite gains the favour of the one-tusked lord.

01-031.json.summary: Sumantu explains the three kinds of the fourth lunar day. The Shiva fourth, in the bright fortnight of Bhadrapada, is honoured by women with gifts of jaggery, salt and cakes, and is said to multiply bathing, giving, fasting and recitation a hundredfold by Ganesha's grace. The Shanta fourth is in Magha and gives peace and a thousandfold fruit. The Sukha fourth, when it falls on a Tuesday, gives beauty and happiness. He tells how the blood-drop of Shiva and Uma fell on the earth in the Himalaya and became Angaraka (Mars). One who fasts and eats at night on this day worships Mars with red flowers and ointment, after worshipping Ganesha, and says prayers and mantras: bathing, touching durva grass, the shami tree, the ashvattha tree and a cow, and offering sesame, barley and ghee in the fire. A golden or silver image of Mars with Vinayaka is set up in a copper vessel and given to a Brahmin reciter with a fee. He warns against stinginess when one has wealth. The reward is beauty like the sun, and a place in the world of Mars.

01-032.json.summary: Sumantu says the fifth lunar day is dear to the Nagas, who give fearlessness to those who bathe them with milk. Shatanika asks why their mother cursed them. Sumantu tells how Kadru and Vinata made a wager about the colour of the horse that rose from the churning, and Kadru asked her sons to hang on its tail to make it look dark. When they refused, Kadru cursed them to be burned in a serpent sacrifice by Janamejaya. Brahma comforts the grieving Vasuki, telling him the sage Jaratkaru will marry his sister of the same name, and their son Astika will stop the sacrifice. Brahma gave the fifth day to the Nagas for their joy. Sumantu gives the vow: honour the Nagas with offerings and food for Brahmins, eat sweet food first, and the reward is a place among the Nagas, a good birth and no snake fear for the family. A person whose relative died of a bite should keep twelve fifth days in a year, with a night meal on the fourth, honouring five Nagas with flowers and incense and naming one Naga each month. Shatanika's father Parikshit did this, and Shatanika is told to give a golden serpent and a cow to Vyasa.

01-033.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the kinds, colours and marks of serpents, their fangs and the amount of poison. Sumantu describes the number of eggs, the types of fangs and the way a serpent bites, and the effects on a person who is bitten. He also tells how bites differ by serpent kind and by how many times a serpent bites, and which bites are beyond cure, such as those of a four-fanged serpent. He gives these as knowledge for those who treat poison.

01-034.json.summary: Kashyapa tells the signs of a person bitten at the wrong time by death. These include a broken neck, an upward stare, a crow-foot shaped wound, trembling and red eyes. The chapter lists the days and places that are dangerous, such as the eighth, ninth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, empty houses and burning grounds, and twelve vital spots. It describes how the messenger who comes for help, and the time of day, show whether the person will live. Serpents are linked with the sun and moon in this system.

01-035.json.summary: Kashyapa continues on poison: how it travels to the head, the signs when it reaches the skin, blood, phlegm or wind, and the changes of colour in the body. He says what the signs of each stage are and when the bitten person cannot be saved. He ends by naming a medicine that can restore life and which should be given quickly.

01-036.json.summary: Gautama asks how to tell the bite of a male snake, a female snake, a young snake, a snake with young, or a eunuch-type snake. Kashyapa answers: the victim's eyes look up, down, left or right, and signs such as sweating, shivering or body ache differ with the kind of snake. Female snakes are stronger at night, male snakes by day. He names four kinds of snakes (Darvikara, Mandali, Rajila, Vyantara) and links them to the three humours of the body and to the four classes, with the signs of a bite and a herbal remedy for each class. He names the chief Nagas (Ananta, Vasuki, Takshaka, Karkotaka, Padma, Mahapadma, Shankhapala, Kulika), their colours and directions, and counts 92 kinds of snakes. Sumantu ends by saying that Nagas should be worshipped, above all on the fifth day, and that on the fifth day of Shravana, snake figures drawn in cow dung on both sides of the door bring freedom from fear of snakes.

01-037.json.summary: Sumantu says that in the month of Bhadrapada, on the fifth day, a person should draw Nagas in black and other colours and worship them with scent, flowers, ghee, milk-rice and incense. Takshaka and the other serpents are pleased. The worshipper's family, down to seven generations, need not fear snakes, so a wise person should worship the Nagas with every effort.

01-038.json.summary: Sumantu says that in the month of Ashvina, on the fifth day, a person should make Nagas of kusha grass and worship them with scent and other offerings. They are bathed with ghee, water and milk, and fed with wheat, milk-rice and other foods. Those who do this with purity and devotion please the Nagas, led by Shesha, and gain peace and a long stay in the world of peace. This ends the rule of the fifth day. The mantra "Om kurukulle phat svaha" is given as one that keeps off all serpents.

01-039.json.summary: Sumantu describes the sixth lunar day, which is dear to Kartikeya (Skanda), who became leader of the gods' army on it. A person who eats only fruit, or only one meal at night, on the sixth day, especially in Kartika, will win what he wishes; a king who lost his kingdom regains it soon. He should give water to Skanda facing south, with curd, ghee and flowers, and a short prayer to Skanda. After giving food to a Brahmin, he eats at night using the ground as his plate. Skanda gives success, steadiness, long life and a kingdom, in this world and the next, to the one who keeps the vow and to the one who hears it.

01-040.json.summary: Shatanika finds this vow hard and doubts it. He asks how Kartikeya, who has many births, can be so great, and whether birth or deed makes a person better. Sumantu says Brahma was asked this long ago by sages who saw Vishvamitra's Brahminhood. They ask whether class differences are real or only made up. Brahma answers with reasoned argument: Brahminhood cannot be proved by the senses or by the Veda, a Brahmin is not different from a Shudra as a human being, and the soul cannot be called a Brahmin. He then tells Manu's story of seven hunters who were reborn as deer, ducks, swans and finally as learned Brahmins in Kurukshetra, so class is not fixed. He says class names come from agreement and work, that Brahmins who sell meat, salt or milk, or live badly, become Shudras, and that a Shudra becomes a Brahmin and a Brahmin a Shudra.

01-041.json.summary: Brahma continues his argument on caste. He says that even Shudras, outcastes and demons such as Ravana study the Veda, and that people who go to another country or hide their birth pass as Brahmins, so study cannot mark a difference. The Veda does not purify a person without good conduct, and a Brahmin who has learned four Vedas but lacks conduct is as useless as a eunuch with a jewel of a wife. He says the power to bless or curse, and the rites and marks, are found in all people, and he denies any difference in body, colour, feeling, strength, mind or life between the four classes. All are children of one father, like fruits of one fig tree. Gotra names are shared across classes, and the body, which perishes, cannot itself be Brahminhood.

01-042.json.summary: Brahma continues. He says that proud people, blind with pride in birth, family, looks and learning, wander through countless births and should not boast of birth. He lists the birth rites from conception to marriage, and says rites do not by themselves make a Brahmin, since a person with all the rites who acts badly goes to hell, while one without rites who behaves well is the best Brahmin. He names great sages born of unusual mothers who became Brahmins through austerity: Vyasa (a fisherwoman's son), Parashara (a dog-eater's), Shuka, Kanada, Rishyashringa (a doe's), Vasishtha (a courtesan's), Mandapala and Mandavya. He ends that even those who received all the rites may become great sinners, so Brahminhood is only a matter of agreement.

01-043.json.summary: Brahma continues. He asks whom the rites really improve, the body, which is unclean by nature, or someone else. He lists the faults that make a Brahmin as bad as the worst: cruel deeds, killing a Brahmin, lying with a teacher's wife, stealing, drinking, lying, mocking the Veda, selling the Veda and selling what should not be sold. He says that such people are not made pure even by hundreds of sacrifices, and that Brahmins who do the work of Shudras are Shudras. He says that men and women of the two classes have children together just as within one class, while animals of different kinds do not, and that the unclean body, bound by anger and desire, shows no real difference between the classes. He ends that the human differences are made by agreement only.

01-044.json.summary: Brahma describes the true Brahmin: one who knows what to give up and what to take, has mastered senses, mind and speech, is calm, free from grief and pride, harmless and wishing well to all, and follows the rule laid down by Brahma. Brahmins are named from Brahma (Brahman), Kshatriyas from protecting against harm, Vaishyas from trade and livelihood, and Shudras from those who sorrow and serve. He lists the qualities of a Brahmin, such as patience, self-control, kindness, giving, truth, purity, no envy and no greed, and says that where they are found Brahminhood grows. The natural work of each class is given, and he says a Shudra of good character can be better than a Brahmin of bad conduct, and that one who sells no liquor is a good Shudra.

01-045.json.summary: Brahma says he will state again, briefly, what he has said with reasons for the doubt about birth and deed: people gain success from birth and deed together, just as a task succeeds from fate and effort together. Sumantu says that the great teacher told this to his pupils long ago in brief, and that Brahma answered the sages in this way. He tells Shatanika not to be surprised, because the ways of the gods, especially about Kartikeya, are hard to know.

01-046.json.summary: Sumantu praises the sixth day of Bhadrapada, which is holy, takes away sin and is dear to Guha (Kartikeya). Bathing and giving on it never lose their fruit, and those who see Kartikeya in the south are freed from sins such as killing a Brahmin. He lists the rewards of worshipping Guha with devotion and flowers such as champaka, of building him a strong house of wood or stone, sweeping his house or raising a flag, and of worshipping him with sandal, aloe and camphor. Kings should honour him above all, and one who worships him before battle wins as Indra did over the demons. One should not eat or use oil on the sixth day, and one who eats only at night on it is freed from all sins.

01-047.json.summary: Sumantu describes the seventh day, which belongs to the sun. He tells how the Sun was born with the cosmic egg and got his name Martanda from staying long in the egg; Daksha gave him his daughter Rupa (Samjna) and Vishvakarma showed his form. Unable to bear his fierce heat, she left her shadow Chhaya in her place and went to the northern Kurus as a mare. Chhaya bore Shani and Tapati, favoured them over Yama and Yamuna, and struck Yama; when he raised his foot, she cursed it to be eaten by worms. Martanda softened the curse, made Yamuna and Tapati holy rivers, and learned the truth from Daksha. Vishvakarma trimmed his form on a lathe, red sandal and karavira flowers eased his pain, and as a horse he joined her in the north, where she bore the Ashvins and Revanta. Sumantu then gives the vow of fasting on the seventh with a vegetable meal at night, its rewards, the offerings of three successive breaking-of-the-fast meals, and the hearing of the Purana.

01-048.json.summary: Shatanika asks for the seventh-day rite in detail, and Sumantu retells a talk between Krishna (Vasudeva) and his son Samba. Samba asks how a person can be free from suffering and gain both worldly joys and liberation. Krishna says the grace of a god is the surest means, that the gods can be known by direct sight, by reasoning and by the scriptures, and that the one god seen directly is the Sun, the eye of the world, from whom the world arises and into whom it goes. He says that one who worships the Sun in his disk at dawn, noon and evening reaches the highest state, with mantras and a guarded place, and that this will end all pain of body, nature and the gods.

01-049.json.summary: Krishna gives the best rule for worshipping the sun. He describes bathing with sun mantras, sipping water, giving an offering of water to the sun and meditating on him in the heart. He then describes breath control, the cleansing of the body of faults, and the placing of mantras on the limbs, followed by worship with scents, flowers, red sandal, cooked rice and offerings, in a lotus drawn with the sun at the centre and the planets and world-guardians around. He names five hand signs and says that one who does the worship daily for a year gains his wishes: the sick are freed from disease, the poor gain wealth, a ruined king his kingdom and the childless a son.

01-050.json.summary: Krishna gives the occasional rule for the seventh day, the day of an eclipse and the days of the sun's change of sign. It includes a day-time meal of cooked offering, sleeping on kusha grass, bathing, the fire offering to the sun and a water offering. In each month a different form of the sun is worshipped (Varuna in Magha, then Surya, Dhatri, Indra, Ravi, and others up to Vishnu in Pausha). At the end of a year the worshipper makes a golden chariot with seven horses and a golden image of the sun, honours twelve Brahmins standing for the months, and gives the chariot, parasol, village, cows and land to the teacher. Those who cannot afford gold may make the chariot of copper or flour and still gain a kingdom or long life. Krishna adds that Surya told him this in the first age, that it brought him many sons and victory over demons, and tells Samba to keep it secret.

01-051.json.summary: Krishna continues the rules for the sun's worship on the fifth to seventh days of the bright half. In the months from Magha, one eats once on the fifth, eats at night on the sixth and fasts on the seventh. The sun is worshipped with red sandal, karavira flowers and incense in some months, with white sandal and white flowers in others, and with agastya flowers in Kartika and later months, with milk-rice, sweets and sugar-cane juice offered, and Brahmins fed. Cow dung is eaten and used for bathing to cleanse the body. In Magha the feeding and gifts are doubled, and a chariot procession is made when one can afford it. This is called the Ratha Saptami, a great holy day; one who fasts on it gains wealth, sons, fame and learning.

01-052.json.summary: Krishna disappears from Samba's sight, and Samba keeps the Ratha Saptami and is freed from worry and illness. The story then turns to a question Rudra once put to Brahma on the golden mountain: how the sun goes round in his chariot. Brahma describes the one-wheeled chariot of gold, whose parts stand for the year, seasons, months and days, drawn by seven horses named for the Vedic metres, with Aruna as driver. He tells how the chariot turns on the pole-star and goes through the circles of the sun's path, and he names the gods, sages, singers, dancers, snakes and demons who ride with the sun in each pair of months. Rudra then asks how to bow to the sun in the sky. Brahma gives a short rule: draw a circle on ground smeared with cow dung, call the sun, honour the other gods, walk round and bow flat, and give a gift to a Brahmin, which frees one from disease and sin.

01-053.json.summary: Brahma tells Rudra who serve the sun's chariot: Aruna is the driver, and gods, winds, Nagas, Yakshas, the Valakhilyas and others have fixed places, with Garuda, Varuna and others at the banner and umbrella. The sun and the gods give heat, rain and light and drive away the evil deeds of beings. The sun feeds the gods and ancestors with soma that waxes and wanes with the moon. The sun's chariot, with its seven horses, goes round the earth with one wheel and travels 180-odd circles in a year. Brahma explains how the sun is seen to rise and set in the four quarters of Mount Meru in turn, how many yojanas he covers in a moment, and which gods honour him in turn at dawn, noon, evening and midnight.

01-054.json.summary: Rudra marvels at the glory of the sun (the swan), and asks to hear more. Brahma says the three worlds are made of the sun's power, he is the root of the world and the highest god. Offerings made in the fire reach him, rain comes from him, and from rain food and living beings. All things arise from and return to him, he is the aim of those who meditate and of those who seek liberation, and without him time, seasons, crops and every action would be impossible. The sun is of different colours in the six seasons, and Brahma explains what each colour foretells, such as fear for the army when he is copper-coloured, for the prince when yellow, and for the priest when white. The chapter ends in the middle of these signs.

01-055.json.summary: Rudra asks how the sun's chariot festival should be held, with what rule, at what time and with what reward for those who draw the chariot, dance, sing or keep watch. Brahma says the sun's chariot festival and Indra's festival keep a country free from famine, robbers and trouble. In the month of Bhadrapada, he describes the daily anointing of the sun with ghee and colour, then a bath in Pausha with water from the holy rivers and places, and the keeping of the image in the bathing house. The chariot rides from Magha bright half: a fast on the seventh, a night-long watch, the chariot with the sun and his two queens Rajni and Nikshubha, the teacher Brahmins, a Garuda banner and umbrella, drawn by pure men, never Shudras or drinkers. It goes out by the north gate, then the east, south, west and middle of the town, with a stay and worship at each, and returns home after the fourteenth day. Brahma explains that the chariot festival is allowed because the sun himself travels in a chariot, and that other gods are not to be moved. He ends with a rule that all who come must be fed, and with the prayer for the gods to accept the offering.

01-056.json.summary: Rudra asks how the chariot should be moved and who goes with it. Brahma lists the order of the attendants (Pratihara, Dandanayaka, Pingala, Dindi, Lekhaka) and the care needed to keep the chariot from breaking. He explains the bad omens of a broken part of the chariot, such as fear to Brahmins if the pole breaks, loss of kings if the banner falls, and how to answer them with offerings, fire rites, and the giving of gifts. He then gives the rite for pleasing the nine planets: wood for each planet's fire, gifts such as a red bull for Mars and gold for Mercury, offerings of food to each, and mantras. He says that rulers rise and fall by the planets, so they should be honoured, and the one who suffers should worship the one that troubles him. After the peace rite the chariot is taken on and returns to the temple.

01-057.json.summary: Brahma lists what food and offerings go to each god and group at the chariot festival: milk gruel to Brahma, fruits to Kartikeya, honey and flesh to Vivasvat, sesame food to Yama, flowers and fruits to others, sweets to Ganesha, and so on, with dozens of gods, sages, snakes, ancestors and spirits named. They are to be given three times a day with incense and mantras, and sesame offered to Brahmins for peace. When the festival ends, the image is taken down from the chariot to the circle, a lamp-waving rite is done against the evil eye, and the image with its two queens is put on the altar for ten days of worship, with a special bath and feast on the fourth day, after which it goes back to its own temple.

01-058.json.summary: Brahma gives the rewards of the chariot festival. One who does or has it done lives long in the sun's world, is not born poor or sick, and gains the world of a particular god according to what he gives: ghee for anointing, water from the holy rivers, coloured food, sweeping and decorating the road, dancing and singing, keeping the night watch, or giving servants. Seeing the sun's chariot is hard to get. If the festival was missed one year, it is to be held in the twelfth year, and those who stop it are called Mandehas, demons. Brahma adds that the sun is made of the Veda, the metres and all gods, and so is carried by Brahmins and others who fast, never by Shudras. The sun is to be honoured before other gods. The days of seeing the sun at the festival, such as full and new moon, the sixth and seventh, and the months Ashadha, Kartika and Magha, are specially holy. Hearing the festival story frees from disease, and Brahma ends by turning to the seventh day again.

01-059.json.summary: Brahma tells Rudra more about the Ratha Saptami in Magha. One fasts on the sixth, worships the sun with scent and flowers, sleeps before him, and on the seventh worships him again, feeds Brahmins, and avoids stinginess. At the end of the year the chariot festival is held by the rule given earlier. A golden chariot is made on a copper plate with gems set in each direction (ruby in the middle, pearl east, sapphire south, emerald west, coral north) and cloths of several colours, then decorated and offered to the teacher who knows the Saptami rite. If gold cannot be had, one makes it of silver, copper or flour. The rewards: one becomes a follower of the sun, the classes rise to a higher state, a girl gains a learned husband, a childless woman a son, and a widow is spared widowhood in other births. Hearing it frees from the sin of killing a Brahmin.

01-060.json.summary: Brahma goes away after speaking of the chariot festival, and the speaker (in the voice of a devotee asking to learn) says he has heard much of the glory of the sun, from whom Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva are born. He praises the sun: only that tongue is blessed that praises Martanda, only that mind that is fixed on the sun, and only those hands that worship him; one bow to the sun carries a person across the sea of rebirth. He asks to be taught how to worship him, by what mantras, secrets, gifts, vows, fasts and offerings.

01-061.json.summary: The speaker (Sumantu) bows to the sun and retells what Brahma once said to the sages about worshipping him. The sages had asked for a way to liberation that is easy in this age, since the stopping of the mind's movements is hard and life is short. Brahma taught them the yoga of action: worship the sun daily with offerings, bowing, service, vows, fasts and feeding Brahmins, with the mind fixed on him and all actions given to him. This frees from rebirth. The sages then wrote books on this yoga. The chapter ends with the instruction: when you rise, walk, eat and sleep, think of the sun, and you will cross the sea of rebirth.

01-062.json.summary: Sumantu tells of a talk between the sun and Dindi, who was weighed down by the sin of killing a Brahmin. Dindi praised the sun with a hymn, and the sun, pleased, offered a boon. Dindi asked that his sin go and that he be taken across the sea of rebirth. The sun taught the seedless yoga that ends sorrow, but Dindi said he could not master his senses. The sun then taught the yoga of action: be devoted to him, see him in all beings, make an image of him in gold, silver, stone, clay or wood and worship it, think of him while moving, standing and eating, and give him what is dear. The sun adds that this frees from the sin of killing a Brahmin and from rebirth. Dindi asks him to explain the yoga of action in full, the sun promises, and disappears.

01-063.json.summary: Dindi goes to Brahma and asks him to explain the yoga of action. Brahma says the sin of killing a Brahmin is gone by the sun's sight alone, and that to worship the sun one must be initiated, which comes after many births when sin is almost used up. Those who dislike the sun or the Veda and Brahmins show their sin, while those whose sin is nearly gone gain faith. A person who harms no being in deed, thought or word, bows to Brahmins and gods, and sees everything as the sun is fit for initiation. Brahma lists the rewards of worship: making an image or a temple of the sun, giving flowers, incense, ointments, bathing the image with water, honey, ghee and milk, singing and music. He says Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra and the sages all gained their powers by worshipping the sun, and tells Dindi to please him with fasts for a year.

01-064.json.summary: Dindi asks how fasts please the sun and what to avoid. Brahma says that a person freed from sin who lives with good qualities, without enjoyments, is keeping a fast, whether for one night, two, three or only a night meal, if he thinks on the sun and says his name. Whatever wish one holds in the heart while fasting, the sun grants. One who cannot find flowers may use leaves or durva grass. He lists rewards for sweeping the sun's temple, smearing it with clay or cow dung, sprinkling water, giving lamps, a banner or sesame oil, singing, and reading aloud a book. Everyone, from the student to the ascetic and from every class, has the sun as his refuge. He then gives a fast of Bhadrapada: a day without asking on the fourth, one meal on the fifth, a fast on the sixth with a night's sleep before the sun, and on the seventh feeding Brahmins and offering fruits, each month for twelve months. At the year's end gifts such as gold fruits, a cow, land, or a temple are given, and the poor may offer fruits of flour and a copper bowl. The Phala Saptami frees from poverty, gives a son to the childless and spares a widow widowhood in later lives.

01-065.json.summary: Brahma lists the fruits of the vows: a seeker of sons gains sons and a seeker of duty gains duty. Dindi asks why oil is not touched on the seventh day. The chapter gives rules for this day: a Brahmin who breaks them is made fit again by three penances. It forbids certain things such as meat and wine, sleeping with a woman, gambling and wandering in the street. It also names the sun and rain-god by the month, advises a gift of gold to a Brahmin who serves the sun, and says that hearing it removes sin and gives the sun's world.

01-066.json.summary: Sumantu says Brahma disappeared after speaking. The chapter then tells of a man devoted to praising the sun with hymns, who knows four Vedas with their branches. He bows to a sage, and the sage Durvasas, who is quick to anger, is once mocked by mistake. The man asks by whom he can be freed from disease, and asks who is the god of the gods and the father of the ancestors. The answer is the sun, the father of the ancestors and the god of gods. It ends by promising to speak of the sun's secret.

01-067.json.summary: Brahma tells how he spoke to the god and received an answer. The god is described as beyond the senses and their objects, as present everywhere with hands, feet, eyes, heads and mouths on every side, and as the self of all and source of all. He is likened to the one wind that stays in the body in five forms. When a person knows the self, that person becomes single and free. Even those in heaven bow to him.

01-068.json.summary: Brahma lists ways of pleasing the sun, who has the discus form of Keshava: worship with jasmine flowers, with the kimshuka flower, sweeping and plastering the temple, giving oil of the mahua tree, and bowing to the sun. He says nothing pleases the sun more than these. He speaks of gifts and the rewards: one gift brings wealth, two bring health. He closes with the rule for the seven seventh days, and says the person reaches the sun after death.

01-069.json.summary: Brahma describes dreams. A person who goes to sleep thinking of the god of gods may see signs that foretell the future. It lists favourable dreams, such as seeing a white lotus, a fan or a mirror, climbing a good tree, a fire consuming one's body, riding horses, bulls, lotuses and white elephants, and receiving blessings from bright women. It says that people who are sick and see these signs are freed from their illness.

01-070.json.summary: Brahma ends the account of the seventh-day vows. He says that if Brahmins who are learned in the Puranas and histories are not available, others may be fed. A person who keeps the seven seventh days with devotion gains what is hard to get in the world, including freedom from disease and, for a barren woman, children and grandchildren. He says this sage's tale is told to Dindi and gives the benefit of hearing it with a focused mind, and a prayer to the sun who clears the world's darkness.

01-071.json.summary: Brahma gives a hymn of salutations to the sun under many names, including Surya, Ravi, Prabhakara, Mitra, Dhata, Vidhata, Aryaman and Varuna, and the one with a single-wheeled chariot. He says that one who recites these names of the sun, pure and attentive, at dawn and dusk is freed from sickness and bondage. It is called a secret prayer and a form of the twilight devotion.

01-072.json.summary: Sumantu says the yogi heard Brahma's words about the sun. Shatanika asks where the sun's first place is in Jambudvipa. Sumantu says the sun has three places on this continent, including the city called Samba on the bank of the Chandrabhaga river. He says the twelve Adityas are said to shine there. The chapter then begins the story of why Samba, Krishna's son, was cursed by his father: he had mocked a sage and imitated his gait.

01-073.json.summary: Sumantu tells how the sage Narada visits Krishna and speaks of Samba, whose fate, it says, follows from a curse that must come about. Krishna thinks it over and speaks to Narada. The chapter mentions a pleasure pond with lotuses, a warning that Krishna's wives stay out of sight, and a curse of leprosy placed on Samba. It also has a curse that those women would fall to robbers' hands. Krishna adds that kind words should be spoken, and the chapter ends with Samba regaining his form and health from the sun.

01-074.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the sun's twelve forms, as Samba set up the sun on the bank of the Chandrabhaga. Sumantu says Brahma is beginningless, endless and eternal, and describes the twelve forms of the sun, naming Dhata (second), Tvashta (fifth), Bhaga (seventh), Vishnu (tenth) and Varuna among them. This is called the first, holy place of Mitra. The chapter says a person who worships through these twelve forms is freed from all sins and reaches the sun's world.

01-075.json.summary: Shatanika asks how Samba came to the sun and who led him there. Samba, afflicted by his father's curse, asks Krishna what he did wrong, begs him to withdraw the curse and shows grace. The father says the sun, with twelve forms, is the lord of the world, as Narada has told him. Samba then visits Krishna at Dvaraka and asks which god is to be praised by all. The answer is that the god to be praised, bowed to and worshipped is the sun.

01-076.json.summary: Narada tells that in his travels he once went to the world of the sun. Yakshas, Rakshasas and serpents guard it with weapons raised, and the three twilights stand there in bodily form. The Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts and Ashvins are there. The sun's charioteer is the elder brother of Garuda, and seven green horses, which are the Vedic metres, pull the chariot. Pingala is the scribe and another is the commander. Samba asks how many rays and forms the sun has and what Pingala writes, and asks Narada to explain.

01-077.json.summary: Narada explains the sun to Samba. The supreme Person has no smell, colour, taste, sound or touch, and no form. His image is marked by knowledge and detachment, and the three states of the self-born one are told. The sun is called unborn because he is the first god, and the Prajapati who guards all creatures. The chapter says that in the single ocean after the world's dissolution the golden-egg Person arises beyond darkness, and the waters are called "nara" by the seers.

01-078.json.summary: Narada continues on the sun's nature. After a night equal to a thousand ages, Brahma creates again; Kashyapa is born as the son of Marichi. The chapter describes the heat and light in the sun and fire, the groups of rays, the names of the sun in the twelve months, and the twelve Adityas such as Vishnu, Dhata, Bhaga, Pusha, Mitra, Indra, Varuna and Aryaman. It says the sun is the Vedas and the sacrifices and compares the many forms of the sun to a crystal that takes on colours.

01-079.json.summary: Sumantu says Samba was delighted at hearing all this. The chapter describes the offerings to the ancestors and gods, the sister of Brihaspati, and then the children of the sun. It tells of the maiden Tapati and of how a curse arose, and of the sun's attendants Pingala and the commander being sent. It ends with the origin of the Tapi river, flowing from the foot of the Vindhya, and says a person is freed from all sins and reaches the world of the sun.

01-080.json.summary: Sumantu says that after hearing the divine tale of the sun's greatness, Narada tells of a question once put to Brahma. The chapter lists the fruits of hearing the histories and Puranas and of going around the sun with devotion. Dindi asks for the seventh-day rule in detail, and the story continues with a worshipper who offers perfume and flowers every day. The god tells the worshipper to take up the seventh-day rule and tell a Brahmin. The reward is prosperity, health and many sons.

01-081.json.summary: Brahma gives the rule for the seventh day of the bright fortnight when it falls on a Sunday. One eats one meal on the fifth, a night meal on the sixth, and fasts, sleeps on the ground before the god, worships the lord of the planets, makes the fire offering, gives gifts and then sends the Brahmins away. Incense of the vijaya kind pleases the sun. Gifts and offerings made on this day never decay, and merely remembering it gives merit.

01-082.json.summary: Dindi asks about those who worship the sun on a Sunday. Brahma says they gain health in this world and go to the sun's world. He gives a mantra named Mahashveta, which brings the wished fruit, and the names Nanda, Bhadra, Saumya and others. The worshipper becomes a king and is freed from sin and fear. Some say the night meal should be taken after seeing the stars. He gives gifts of barley with jaggery and ghee, and promises that no poverty or disease will enter the family of one who does this.

01-083.json.summary: Brahma describes the worship of the sun on a certain seventh day, with a night meal or a fast. One offers jasmine flowers and white sandal, gives a fee according to means, and then eats in silence. One who worships the remover of darkness in this way is freed from all sins and goes to the sun's world. Even hearing it frees a person from sin.

01-084.json.summary: Brahma gives the worship of the sun on a further seventh day. Bathing, giving, recitation, fire offerings and offerings to the ancestors and gods are done, with a night meal. Red lotuses and red sandal are offered. The text says he who worships the bright, multicoloured lord of rays in this way gains the result.

01-085.json.summary: Brahma describes the next seventh day. The worshipper offers oleander flowers mixed with red sandal and a food offering of rice with sesame, strongly flavoured. The sun, honoured by mantras, grants a son to one who wishes for a son, wealth to one who wants wealth and other desires. He mentions a gift of cakes to the sun.

01-086.json.summary: Brahma gives the rule of a seventh day with a fast and an offering to the ancestors. The worshipper honours the sun at night in front of the image, rises in the morning, bathes and gives the best offering of water. He feeds Brahmins and offers rice balls. One who fasts and performs the ancestor rite on this day surely gains a son, radiant like a Brahmin and as beautiful as a lotus. A night meal, bathing, giving and recitation on that day are said to be a hundredfold in merit.

01-087.json.summary: Brahma says that on the next seventh day the worship of the sun gives a thousandfold fruit. The sun is bathed with ghee, milk and sugarcane juice, with guggul incense and a sweet cake as the food offering. One who worships the sun with this mantra gains the reward.

01-088.json.summary: Brahma says that on this seventh day all the fruit of a holy act is multiplied ten million times. Bathing, giving, recitation, fire offerings and worship of ancestors and gods all are increased a crore-fold when the lord of rays is worshipped. The worshipper gains lordship over the seven worlds through the seven rays.

01-089.json.summary: Brahma describes a seventh day that falls on a Sunday. One takes a single meal and stands facing the sun until it sets, holding a smooth, straight, firm staff four cubits long. The worshipper honours the sun with perfume, flowers and offerings. The result is wealth, grain, a son, health and fame.

01-090.json.summary: Brahma gives the last of this set of seventh-day rules. One takes a night meal, worships the god with devotion and recites the "heart of Aditya" a hundred and eight times. At home one feeds Brahmins according to one's means. The person who worships the sun in this way gains light and fame like his.

01-091.json.summary: Brahma describes another sun worship. The worshipper honours the sun with fragrant pastes, offers flowers of the arka plant held in an arka leaf cup, gives a sweet milk dish, and sleeps on the ground at night. He is freed from all diseases and reaches the sun's abode.

01-092.json.summary: Brahma gives the rule for an eclipse of the sun. One fasts, stays pure and worships the lord of the worlds, the remover of darkness. A fire rite with sesame and ghee is done at a prepared altar outside, and Brahmins are made to recite. All holy acts done then bring good results. He says those who observe the sun's day go to the highest place, and that the result is brilliance like the moon.

01-093.json.summary: Brahma lists the merits of various acts of devotion to the sun. These include lighting a lamp, worshipping with lotuses, worship at midnight, offerings on the equinoxes, eclipses and other special days, giving a young cow, giving a chariot with horses, giving a grove of trees with leaves, flowers and fruit, and giving a copy of the Bharata. Each brings a heavenly reward. He also warns against breaking the sun's procession out of folly or anger, and says nothing else gives such nourishment and satisfaction to the sun.

01-094.json.summary: Brahma tells of a man who came to the sun, and of the worship that two people had made. The sun answers a question about the highest rule of action. He explains that he sent a heavenly chariot for a man doing his vow, and that worship of the book and of the reciter, with perfumes and flowers, pleases him as much as a rite for the dead pleases the ancestors. He says the Puranas are dear to him.

01-095.json.summary: Brahma lists faults to avoid in the sun's temple: entering wearing sandals, and passing phlegm, urine or dung there. He says people who watch the sun being bathed with ghee, honey, milk, water and sugarcane juice, and those who perform the bathing, gain merit. Anyone who spoils the bathing goes to the hells called Tamisra and Raurava. Bathing the god with ghee brings a particular reward.

01-096.json.summary: Dindi says the seven seventh days have been told and asks about the offerings on them. Brahma gives the rule of a seventh day called Jaya, with one meal on the fifth, a night meal on the sixth, bathing with mustard seed, eating cow dung product for purification and feeding Brahmins. He mentions sandal and flowers, worship in the rainy season, and a recital of a holy book. He closes by saying this is the seventh named Jaya.

01-097.json.summary: Brahma gives the next seventh-day rule with a single meal on the fifth day and a night meal on the sixth. Brahmins are fed with sweet cakes, and the second breaking of the fast is said to give the fruit of a royal consecration. The third gives a food offering of ghee cakes. The incense called Amrita and a sweet milk dish are used. A seeker of sons gains sons and a seeker of wealth gains wealth, and in the end the worshipper rides a fine heavenly chariot.

01-098.json.summary: Brahma says that four fast-breaking meals are named by the wise. They use guggul incense, an offering of jaggery cakes and, in the months from Margashirsha on, red lotuses, aloe and sandalwood. He gives the names of the god and what is eaten, and says one repeats "may he be pleased" at each. The worshipper may gain victory over enemies and the three aims of life. He also names gifts of horses and banners set with jewels for the sun.

01-099.json.summary: Brahma says that bathing, giving, recitation, fire offerings and worship of the ancestors and gods on this day are blessed. One who bathes the sun with ghee or milk gains a camphor chariot decorated with a net of bells and becomes a king. A person who fasts on this day goes to the sun's world.

01-100.json.summary: Brahma gives another seventh-day vow with one meal on the fifth day and a night meal on the sixth. Incense of camphor and aloe, flowers of palasha and cakes are offered, along with sandal, white lotuses and guggul. He gives the names of the god, which purify people, and says the worshipper reaches the sun's hall and rejoices.

01-101.json.summary: Brahma describes bathing the lord of the gods and anointing him with sandal. He mentions placing pearls on the horn of the image and gifts to be given to Brahmins and the poor, but not to hypocrites and wrongdoers. A person who gives auspicious things on this day will have a good son. He describes a vessel of mixed spices and grapes with a jewel in each corner, and promises the world of Brahma. He also gives the reward for hearing, reciting or teaching the rules of the seventh day.

01-102.json.summary: Sumantu says the seventh day of the sun has been told, and Brahma goes on to the other lunar days. He says the full-moon day is given by the sun for the ancestors, that Ganesha should be worshipped on the fourth day, and that the Vishvedevas are worshipped on the eleventh. He gives rules with mantras and rites for various days and stars, such as worshipping the waters under the star Purvashadha, and says Prajapati when pleased gives cattle. He closes by saying these are the sacrifices briefly told and praises building an image of the sun.

01-103.json.summary: Brahma says that a person who worships the sun daily gains the fruit of sacrifice. He lists offerings of food and fruit, and says that seventy-seven men of Videha reached the highest state by worshipping him. He says that for one who wants a good state out of disgust with rebirth, the sun is the way. One who sweeps the sun's temple inside and out will reach a jewelled heavenly chariot, and one should also honour the reciter. He ends by saying the sun is the final refuge of all stages of life.

01-104.json.summary: Brahma tells of fasts for wishes and a prayer to be repeated one hundred and eight times in worship, with the name Hamsa and a plea to be the way for those without one. After bathing and worship one repeats the names Hamsa, Martanda and Bhaskara, and reaches the heavenly dwelling of Hamsa after death. He says hearing the tale or music of the sun brings the best state, and that the white seventh day gives a good state to the faithful. Reading or hearing this removes sin and fear.

01-105.json.summary: Brahma describes a sun-fast with fire offerings of ghee. He lists the months of Phalguna, Chaitra, Vaishakha and Jyeshtha as the time of the vow's completion, with sweet offerings given to Brahmins, a special incense, and worship with red lotuses. The sun, pleased, grants wishes. He mentions that Savitri and Aditi gained sons through such a fast, and that a person gains any wish he thinks of while fasting. A traveller who returns and keeps it also gains the fruit.

01-106.json.summary: Vishnu asks about the great lunar days Vijaya, Atijaya and Jayanti, and about the northern course of the sun, which is held best for sun worship. Brahma says that worshipping the sun on that day and fasting with a steady mind brings great merit. One who recites the Rigveda in front of the sun, and gives gifts in his name, gains the fruit of the Samaveda and Yajurveda as well. Such people shine like stars and go to the sun's city.

01-107.json.summary: Brahma says that the northern course of the sun is to be known as the step of Vamana. A person who worships the sun daily in that period, with fine cloths, flowers, incense and ointments, gains the fruit. The chapter includes a vow in which the worshipper swears that if he ever speaks falsely or dies within six months while reciting, may the consequences fall on him. Brahma closes by describing the rule of keeping this vow and worshipping the two feet of the god.

01-108.json.summary: Brahma says a devotee of the sun should not talk with hypocrites and the like. He gives the fast-breaking meals for six months beginning with Magha, the three named Sankrantika, Chitrabhanu and Vibhavasu, and the five cow products. One bows to the god, worships properly, and pleases him at the end of each fast. The worshipper eats at night and avoids oil and alkali. By keeping this the devotee gains whatever he wishes in his heart.

01-109.json.summary: Brahma describes a vow with a mantra "Martanda": after worship one repeats the name, gives a fee to a Brahmin and avoids speaking to hypocrites. One takes a cow product to purify the self and keeps fasts through all the months. If this is kept for a year and done properly, the worshipper gains the full fruit and shines with a splendour like that of Shandileya. People still see such persons shining in the world.

01-110.json.summary: Brahma describes worship of the sun with flowers, incense and offerings of water, giving a fee to a Brahmin, and eating at night in silence while remembering and reciting the names of the sun. After the fast is complete, the worshipper honours the teacher of the world. He says hearing the name of the endless one gives unlimited fruit, and that the person goes after death to a heavenly place full of song.

01-111.json.summary: Brahma says the worshipper should not speak with hypocrites, should be self-controlled and should apply the sun's yearly anointing. He gives rules for festival days with musical instruments, conch and trumpet sounds and loud Vedic chanting. He says that one who keeps this rule for twelve months in order gains the fruit of worshipping the sun.

01-112.json.summary: Brahma says the sun is not pleased by killing living things, nor by flowers or fruit alone, and that in a mind spoiled by passion the darkness does not clear. The sun is pleased naturally by one who does no harm. He lists gifts on a lunar day: a diamond, sesame, rice, barley, gold, water, a water pot, sandals, and says that a person who worships the teacher of the world on that day gains birth in a good family, health and wealth. He urges the listener to worship the sun with care.

01-113.json.summary: Vishnu asks Brahma again about the fruit of acts of service and of song and music in the sun's worship. Brahma says one who builds a temple of the sun, of wood or stone, lifts a hundred generations of his family before and after him, and enjoys heaven for sixty thousand years. A temple should be built on a fine piece of ground. The chapter also tells that Yama once instructed his servants not to take those who are devoted to the sun, who worship with flowers, incense, clothes and ornaments, or whose family built his temple.

01-114.json.summary: Brahma says that one who bathes the sun's image with ghee gains the fruit of giving a hundred cows to Brahmins. He mentions King Bhuridyumna, who won the seven-continent earth, and gives the days for ghee bathing, such as the dark eighth and the sixth and seventh days. The sun is made of all sacrifices and ghee is the best offering. The worshipper gains joy, health, beauty, the good will of the planets, strength and the love of all people.

01-115.json.summary: Brahma and Kaushalya speak about the reward of sun worship. Those who do it gain calm of mind, gentleness and comfort in the body. The chapter lists good perfumes and incenses, saffron, tagara, karnikara, bilva and shami leaves, and fine cloths of silk and cotton, to be offered. It tells the worshipper to think of himself as the sun when he offers the sacrifice.

01-116.json.summary: Brahma tells a long story of a king who pleased the sages and of what they say about his earlier birth. The sage Paravasu answers the king's question on how people worship the sun in their houses and gives a variety of vows. The chapter praises the continuing practice of sprinkling and anointing, with offerings of perfumes, aloe, camphor, sandal and saffron, and the reading of histories and Puranas by reciters.

01-117.json.summary: Aruna asks why the Bhojakas, the sun's priests, are dear to the sun. The sun answers that their work is the worship of himself. He explains how he had a temple built on this continent, how the king son of Priyavrata was told to act on his word, and how the Bhojakas came to be named because they do not eat unfit food. The sun says that only a Bhojaka should install an image, and he warns that if anyone gives to Shudras or Vaishyas out of greed, or offers flawed flowers, he will destroy that family. It ends with a king worshipping the sun with his wife.

01-118.json.summary: Brahma tells of a man named Bhadra who is asked by sages to explain his story. He tells of a temple of the sun built on the bank of the Sarayu, of a man with a wicked mind toward the sun, and of how he became sick with fear and disease after offending the Bhojakas. The chapter says that even a leper Shudra gained the best Brahminhood through the sun's worship. It says whoever gives a lamp to the temple in Kartika gains merit and that one who wants good should give lamps and not take them away.

01-119.json.summary: Brahma tells a story in which a man reflects on how people spend their lives for sons, wives, houses and fields without knowing time or themselves. He marvels at the power of delusion, which clings even in hell, and how the mind keeps clinging to sense objects. He asks the one before him, a good man, to tell what deeds have been done, so as to understand his present state. The chapter ends with Brahma telling Krishna about those who are blind, mute, deaf or lacking discernment and the gifts that remove such conditions.

01-120.json.summary: Vishnu asks Brahma about beings troubled by poison, disease and other afflictions. Brahma says that when a person's sins are worn away, he turns to the Vedas and the twice-born. One who always honours the Brahmins who serve the sun is freed from fear of rebirth, and one who has a heart-pleasing image of the sun made, or gives wicks and offerings, gains his wish. Such people gain heavenly lands of curd, milk and honey and shine like the moon, surrounded by the gods.

01-121.json.summary: Shatanika notes that the drawing of the sun's body has been briefly told. Brahma comes and bids the work proceed. The sun is set on the earth and praised: "may you be well, lord of the world". Indra comes and praises him as the refuge of all beings in whom all is established, who alone created and woke the world. The chapter describes singing and music with the vina and flute and all the gods bowing with hands on their foreheads. It ends with a verse praising the sun as honoured by Shiva, Brahma and Vishnu.

01-122.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the time when the sun was being drawn. Sumantu tells him to listen with one mind. The chapter is a hymn of praise to the sun, saluting him as the one who helps those who bow, the revealer of the world, the giver of many boons, the unborn, the soul of beings and lord of rays, the light of the gods and the benefactor of the world. It says he rides his chariot always for the good of the world, and that the god was thus praised by Brahma long ago.

01-123.json.summary: Shatanika asks for more of the story of the sun. Vishnu, Shiva and others stood by while the sun was praised as having hands, feet, eyes, heads and mouths on every side. The gods praise him and ask for relief, as they find no peace in heaven, earth or sky. They honour Tvashtri, the maker, in thought, word and deed. A hymn made by the three gods is given, to be recited at both twilights, and the sun is praised by gods and divine sages. Sumantu says the whole account of the sun has been told.

01-124.json.summary: Brahma tells how the sun's attendants (the Pramathas) asked him why he travels without rest. There are eighteen of these attendants and fourteen others riding with the sun. The sages say they should become his chief helpers to remove hindrances. The chapter explains the names of those who record the good and bad deeds of people, and gives word-roots for names like Yama and Kalmasha. It names Raivata and Dindi as standing in front of the sun, and ends by saying the best have been named. Sumantu then speaks.

01-125.json.summary: Shatanika asks about the gods of the present and coming ages. Sumantu names the present gods, among them Hara and Tryambaka, and the future ones. He says Dharma is a son of Brahma, that Indra is now Ojasvin and Bali will follow, and he speaks of the fires with their sons and grandsons. He names the planets, including Rahu as the son of Simhika and Ketu as the son of Brahma, and explains the star circle with Jupiter, and the heights of the Pole Star above the earth. He closes by saying a person who worships the sky with devotion is blessed.

01-126.json.summary: Sumantu lists the words for the sky and the mountains, the Himalaya, Hemakuta, Nishadha and Nila, and the elements in order: fire, air and sky, and then the origin of elements. He tells of the layers around the world-egg and the Person who is lord, by whom the world is covered. He describes golden Mount Meru with four sides and four peaks, one called Saumanasa, with Brahma in the middle, and the planets and lights around it. Shiva is placed at a peak and the Vayavya peak is honoured by all gods and said to be made of the Vedas.

01-127.json.summary: Shatanika asks how Samba of boundless power worshipped the sun. Samba, overcome with his disease, goes to the holy place called Mitravana, famous in the three worlds, and praises the sun, calling him the great Person shining in the sun's disc, who is time itself and the protector of all beings. The god, pleased, grants Samba a wish, and tells him more. Having given Samba this boon and another to the lion of the Vrishnis, the sun says that one who worships him with devotion goes to the sun's world.

01-128.json.summary: Sumantu says Samba, thin and covered with veins, praised the sun. Seeing him suffering, the sun speaks to Krishna's son and gives him a hymn of names of the sun, among them Vaikartana, Vivasvan, Martanda, Bhaskara and Ravi, witness of the worlds, lord of the three worlds, creator, destroyer, and destroyer of darkness. The hymn gives health, wealth and fame. One who recites it at dawn and dusk is freed from wrong done in mind, speech and body. It also says to recite it when giving food, bathing, bowing and circling, and Samba praises the sun with this king of hymns.

01-129.json.summary: Sumantu tells that Samba, having received the sun's boon, made an image of the sun's disc and bathed daily with faith. He bowed to Prabhavati and took her from the water and set up the sun's image. The image speaks to Samba, saying that its earlier form had too strong a light, and that it was remade with skill. The god says this holy place has been made to carry Samba across, and that people will see his presence there on the shore in the forenoon. Samba, hearing this from the sun, was glad.

01-130.json.summary: Shatanika asks how Samba set up the sun's image. Narada gives rules for building a temple of the sun: a fine site, the right measurements with a sixty-four-square plan, the proportions of image and base, and the sizes of a temple of many floors with four doors and many spires. He says the temple should be in the middle of a city and describes its parts and the placing of the shrines of the Ashvins outside the first god's house. The founding is to be marked by conch, trumpet and music. He ends by saying that the rule for the sites of the gods has been told in order.

01-131.json.summary: Narada gives the rule for making an image of the sun. He lists the trees fit for wood: those that are not milky, weak or in unseasonal flower, two trees for each class in order, including kesara, sarja, mango and sala. He rejects trees fallen of themselves or felled by elephants. The sculptor, wearing white clothes, prays to the tree before cutting it, and worships and touches it at night. At dawn the tree is worshipped again, and the way it falls is read for omens: a silent fall without catching is held best.

01-132.json.summary: Narada gives the marks of images of the gods. An image of one hand is gentle, one of two hands gives wealth. The body is measured by eighty-four finger-widths, with exact sizes for eyes, arms, legs, shoulders, forehead and nose. The chapter describes the sun with a bright disc and jewelled earrings, wearing a coat, with a lotus-like glow and a pleasant face. It tells which faults bring harm, such as a cracked or damaged image causing fear of weapons or death, and an image leaning to the wrong side that harms the owner's wife or life.

01-133.json.summary: Narada describes the rite of consecrating the image. Colours are given by direction: red toward the south-east and black toward the south and south-west. An image of copper brings growth of children. Samba then asks Narada to tell how the sun contains all gods. Narada says the elder of the gods is his head, Brihaspati his skull, Sarasvati lives in his tongue, the sages in the pores of his skin, the seas in his belly, Meru in the middle of his back, and the seven lower worlds in his nails. The chapter closes with how images are placed according to the body's parts.

01-134.json.summary: Narada gives the days and stars for setting up the image: the first, second, fourth and fifth lunar days, certain stars such as Revati and Ashvini. He describes the tent, ten cubits on every side, with a square fire pit in the east, fires of several woods, the mantra for the west side, grain in dishes, cloths and ornaments, and a great festival with auspicious sounds and cries of victory. Banners are given to Indra in the east and to the lord of Yakshas in the north-east, and a white umbrella and curd are placed at the centre.

01-135.json.summary: Narada gives the rule for the image's bathing. Water from the holy Sarasvati, Chandrabhaga and Sindhu rivers is placed on the pots and offered to the sun with prayers. The sixth pot is filled with water from the south-west. The five cow products are brought in a copper vessel, and water is strained through cloth with the Vedic verse to Jatavedas. The image is bathed with milk and then with milk-rice, and one is shown how to take food that has touched the ground. The chapter ends by saying which bathers should be avoided.
