At the end Vetala puts a question about duty and a woman who left her faultless bride, which the king answers.

06-002.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story set on the Yamuna bank at Dharmasthali, where King Gunadhipa rules. His sister Madhumati is named, and a wise young man, Vamana, goes to Kashi to study. Three Brahmins, Vamana, Trivikrama and Keshava, with the names Harisharma and Satyashila, love the girl Sushila. On a day in Magha, the auspicious time is set. The girl dies and Harisharma does all the rites. Trivikrama grieves much, and Keshava takes her bones. At Sarayu a Brahmin named Ramasharma, devoted to Shiva, with his wife Vishalakshi, brings a dead child back to life with a mantra. The bones are given to a Brahmin, who revives the girl. Vetala asks Vikramaditya which of them should have her, and he answers that the one who gave life is like a father.

06-003.json.summary: Suta tells of a story set in the city of Vardhavan. Vidvanmala, devoted to her husband, is named. A man gives a thousand gold pieces a day, spends part, and keeps the rest. To test him, a crying woman is sent to the burning ground, and the hero Viravara, skilled in weapons, goes toward the sound and speaks gently. Rajalakshmi says she will die at the end of the month, and the goddess says the head of his son must be offered to Chandika. His faithful wife and his son agree. Viravara cuts off his son's head, and the king, seeing all, is moved. The pleased goddess restores the king and grants a boon, and Viravara's family live.

06-004.json.summary: Suta tells the story of King Rupavarman and a bird in a fine cage at his house. Chandravati, the daughter of the king of Magadha, is mentioned, and a salutation to Shiva, the calm giver of wishes. A Brahmin speaks, and Chandravati prays to Durga, who gives wishes. Marriage is arranged in a month. Menaka says to the king that marriages are of this kind. A childless man who performs sacrifices and has a devoted wife is mentioned. A son loses wealth by wrong paths, tells his father robbers took it, and murders his wife for her ornaments. Shridatta goes on trade to Kurukshetra and returns after three months. A thief called Kaphalla sees the cause. Vikrama answers that a woman is more sinful and the man less guilty.

06-005.json.summary: Suta tells of a story in Ujjayini. The messenger Haridasa is a devotee of Hari. His beautiful lotus-eyed daughter asks her father to listen, and he goes to King Harishchandra of the Telugu country. The king asks when Kali will come, and Haridasa answers: when duty told in the Veda is seen reversed, when the rich fall under greed, the Shudras rise, and the earth is barren. A clever Brahmin, a wise Mukunda (Haridasa's son) and the learned Vamana, who shoots by sound, are rivals for the daughter, who is carried off by a Rakshasa to the Vindhya mountain. They fly in a swift chariot given by the goddess. One kills the Rakshasa with an arrow. The three quarrel over the girl, and Vetala's question is who is fit for her. The answer is that the one who kills the Rakshasa is fit.

06-006.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story of King Dharmashila, who has a minister named Andhaka, skilled in logic. Durga is set up by Dharmashila, and at midnight Mahagauri tells him to choose a boon. He praises her as Mahalakshmi and Mahakali and is promised a strong, mighty son. A man goes with Kashidasa to the village of Dharmapura, and meets a girl tired on the road with her father. A lovesick man prays to Chandika, and the girl, the daughter of a washerman, is married after the father is deluded. Kashidasa hears and hurries. A woman offers her head to the goddess and takes the form of the goddess. The goddess grants a boon. A woman asks to be given back her husband, and a fine head was cut by her from two people.

06-007.json.summary: Suta tells of Champapuri, where King Champakesha has a daughter Trilokasundari, with deer eyes, cuckoo voice and a soft body. At her bride-choosing, many kings come, and four of them, called Indra, Yama, Kubera and Varuna, each speak to the king. They are said to be a man bringing jewels for sacrifice, a man for the fire offering and a man for good food each day. The king is bewildered, and the goddess, ashamed, is deluded by fate. Vetala laughs and asks the king. The answer is that the Brahmin who knows all the scriptures is a Brahmin by class, but the one who knows the arts is a Shudra, and the one who knows archery is the king.

06-008.json.summary: Suta tells another Vetala story. King Gunadhipa, rich in wealth and grain, lives in Mithila country for his livelihood. He goes hunting, follows a tiger's track, and, faint with hunger, kills a deer. A man in the story tells the king he has eaten a thousand coins of his and asks a hundred coins a month for his family. At the sea shore the king sees an image of a goddess, a Gandharva's daughter, who speaks to a lover. A woman asks the king to take her in a Gandharva marriage, and the king's servant Chirandeva is also named. She is ashamed when the king says Chirandeva is like a son to him and that she is like a daughter-in-law. Vetala asks the king a question on the highest duty of kings and the servant's deed.

06-009.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story set in Kamapura, where Virasimha is king. A proud merchant, Hiranyadatta, lives there, and a woman who loves flowers walks past a strong man, Dharmadatta's son. In a lonely place she tells him politely that she will go to him on the tenth day after her marriage. He agrees, leaves her and goes home. On the ninth day her husband seizes her by force. She weeps, and a friend asks the reason. She says she is bound by her promise and goes at night to him. On the way a thief asks for her ornaments. She tells him what happened, he lets her pass, and she goes to the man. Fear of widowhood brings her back to her friend, and the thief gives her up out of fear of truth. Vetala asks which of them acted best.

06-010.json.summary: Suta tells of the dutiful king Gunashekhara. Once he goes to Shiva's temple and a scorpion stings him in anger. A fearless man draws the poison out, and speaks about six inner enemies: delusion, pride, arrogance, possessiveness, desire and blame. He says that Vishnu, Rudra and Brahma are bound by illusion, and that the true Jina, who is non-dual and spotless, is not conquered. He teaches worship of the cow, no harm to creatures, and no meat or drink, and the king takes up the Jain way. His grieving queen takes refuge in Shiva and by Rudra's boon bears a fine son. Gunashekhara dies and goes to hell, while his father gets heaven by his son's duty. The king is later at ease in spring with his queens, and a wife faints when he hands her a lotus. The story ends with the Vedic duty being named as the chief one and the householder living like an ascetic being praised in the Jain books.

06-011.json.summary: Suta tells of Punyapura, where the minister is Satyaprakasha. The king asks how many kinds of joy exist, and is told that the joy of a student is Brahma's joy, that of a forest-dweller is a lesser joy of duty, and that of a renouncer is Shiva's joy, the best. He says there is no joy without a wife in the householder's life, and tells his minister to look for a fitting woman. The minister goes from place to place and finds a girl sitting on a golden tree in the water. The king goes to the sea shore and tells her he has come for her. She says on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight a Rakshasa with a crane vehicle will take her. The king kills the Rakshasa and she says she is the daughter of a Vidyadhara. A great festival follows in the city. It ends with the saying that a king who is a sensualist ruins his kingdom.

06-012.json.summary: Suta tells that Devasvami, a Brahmin who knows the Vedas, worshipped Shiva for a son, and a strong boy named Harisvami was born with a share of the gods. His wife, Rupalavanyika, is as lovely as a goddess. Once in spring with her husband, a Gandharva called Sukala is taken by her beauty. The husband wakes and searches for her, then gives up all sense objects and meditates on Hari. Under a banyan tree an ascetic comes, eats milk-rice that was poisoned and dies, going to Shiva's world. Vetala asks the king who bears the sin of killing a Brahmin. The king answers that a Brahmin gave alms to a hungry man out of fate's confusion, that a person must always suffer the sin he has done himself, and that the sin falls on the one who gave the poison.

06-013.json.summary: Suta tells of a merchant named Dharmadhvaja and a man-eating Rakshasa named Vashara. A pleased Rakshasa speaks to his devotee. A pit is made that confuses men's minds, and a thief steals from the king's house at night and hides the goods in the pit. The guards are deluded by the Rakshasa woman's magic. A man says he is a thief and offers the king a share. At midnight the thief tells the king to go home, as the Rakshasa will eat all men that night. The king brings his wealth and the women. The thief is paraded through the town on a donkey with drumbeats and is to be impaled. The king's daughter, deluded by divine illusion, appears, and the goddess Durga is pleased and revives both. The king explains why the man wept and then laughed.

06-014.json.summary: Suta tells of Chandraprabha, a lovely wife who goes to a flowery wood with her friends and is entranced, and a Brahmin who falls to the ground. A Brahmin sees the beautiful young woman and tells her sorrow to another. A twelve-year-old girl is named. Sudeva, a fine Brahmin, is always in her heart, and he tells her that if she is meant for the best Brahmin, a child will come in four months. A minister's son, deluded by a woman's form, embraces her. A minister named Rajakara has a son Madanalasa. The king gives the bride with wealth by Vedic rule, and Shashi takes the king's daughter home. Vetala asks the king whom the girl belongs to, and the king answers that a field belongs to the farmer and not to the seed-giver. Madanalasa then praises Govinda with a hymn, is freed, and embraces his wife joyfully.

06-015.json.summary: Suta tells of a generous Brahmin at Kanyakubja who asks what to do about his poverty. By the goddess's grace a son named Jimutaketu becomes lord of the Vidyadharas and lives for years in divine pleasures. In an earlier life he was a king in the middle country who hunted, kept a night vigil in Valmiki's hut and heard the story of Rama. A tree speaks to him. On the Malaya mountain a girl called Kamalakshi lives at a Shiva temple, and Jimutavahana, struck by love at the sight of her, prays to the god of love. He is given Vishvavasu as a prince. Jimutavahana weeps where an old woman is grieving for her son who is to be eaten by Garuda. Garuda takes him through the sky, and the girl sees him in the air. Garuda hears him say he came to save the old woman's son, and the god vanishes. Vetala puts a question, and the story ends with Shankhachuda going against his enemy.

06-016.json.summary: Suta tells of a merchant, Ratnadatta, who knows duty and is rich. Seeing a woman's lovely form, he says to the king: "Take her, ocean of kindness, she is made fit for you." King Chandrashekhara, called to counsel his minister Vidura, goes home. He worships with incense, lamps and flowers, and a woman wails in fear. He kills a tiger and rejoices. He goes to the temple of Kamavaruthini, whose image will bring delusion on the king, so he does not marry. A woman who was Balabhadra's wife is named. The king, struck by Kama's arrow, faints and falls. A man says the woman is the daughter of Ratnadatta and the wife of his servant, fit for the king. The angry king says he would go to hell if he took her. The army chief is burnt to ashes. Vetala asks whose merit is greater, and the answer is that the king who conquers desire and keeps duty is greater.

06-017.json.summary: Suta tells of King Mahasena of Ujjayini. His son Gunakara loves wine and meat, is abandoned by his relatives and wanders the earth. A yogi, Kapardin, honours him with a meal from skulls, and calls a Yakshini for hospitality. In the morning she goes to Kailasa. Kapardin teaches him the knowledge that draws a Yakshini. He recites the mantra but the lovely goddess does not come. He lives at home with his parents at night, then goes to Pratibodhi's forest and becomes his pupil. He asks why his beloved Yakshini was not obtained. The answer is that action for success is of three kinds, of the body, of speech and of mind, all three together bring success in this life, and so seekers should do all three. The sage praises him.

06-018.json.summary: Suta tells of a just and generous man devoted to Shiva, and his lovely daughter Dhanavati. In time her daughter Mohini is born, and Dhanavati, widowed and without money, lives at her father's house. A Brahmin named Nyayasharma, who stole a Brahmin's property, is mentioned. A merchant's daughter touches the hand of a man who cries out for Rama, Krishna, Pradyumna and Aniruddha. A Brahmin says he is on the stake for three days. Dhanavati marries her daughter Mohini to him, and he dies and goes to Yama's world. Mohini, young and at her mother's house, is told a verse by a Brahmin asking who sleeps and who wakes, and the Brahmins cannot answer. A kindly sage tells her that beings die and are born every day, and describes how desire arises from resolve and greed from desire. Shiva instructs a king who wants a son. A child with three hands is born and the king is amazed. Vetala says a learned man who wants money is like a teacher.

06-019.json.summary: Suta tells of King Rupadatta of Chitrakuta. At noon on a lake shore, a sage's son sees a girl, their eyes meeting, and the king gains knowledge at the sight. A wise sage tells the king duty that includes compassion: take punishment from the unworthy and gain the fruit of worshipping the worthy, truth in worship of the gods, self-control in worship of the teacher. The sage gives his daughter to the king and goes home. A Rakshasa wants to eat the king's wife and asks for a seven-year-old Brahmin boy to be given for him. The boy laughs loudly at the time of death. The middle son, knowing this, takes refuge in the king, and a Shiva devotee laughs when he sees the king with a sword in hand. Vetala asks why.

06-020.json.summary: Suta tells a Vetala story of a village merchant, Arthadatta, who is busy in trade and gives his daughter in marriage to a merchant named Suvarna. By chance a fine Brahmin comes to the house of Anangamanjari. After a fire offering, a lovely woman's daughter goes to clean, and the girl, her eyes unsteady with passion, gives the Brahmin an appointment. At midnight she waits for him, but by fate he does not come, and she dies. The Brahmin, seeing her lifeless, also dies. Suvarna comes and weeps for his beloved. Vetala asks the king, who answers that a Brahmin is always to be honoured by the merchant class as the form of Brahman, and that Suvarna understood in his heart that his beloved was devoted to Brahmins.

06-021.json.summary: Vetala tells King Vikrama a humble tale. A Brahmin learned in the Vedas lives in a village and has four sons, each given to one of the four parts of life. By fate they lose their wealth, and ask their father why. He tells them gambling spends wealth and is the root of sin, tells one son to leave the company of courtesans and to give up meat and wine, and tells them all to turn to Lord Vishnu and give up unbelief and abuse of the gods. They go to another holy place, and after a year Shiva gives them the knowledge that revives the dead. They find a dead tiger's bones. One casts mantra-blessed water on them, the other pours milk, one pours water, and the unbeliever gives water to the sleeping tiger. Vetala asks who is the greatest fool, and the answer is the one who woke the tiger.

06-022.json.summary: Vetala tells of a Brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and has two sons skilled in all learning. An old man devoted to Shiva, Shambhudatta, makes a joyful fire offering. Liladhara sees a goat about to die and says killing creatures leads to a dreadful hell. He recalls that long ago in the Satya age, Brahmins performed sacrifices and spoke sweetly, but their view gave no fruit. The sages are amazed. In the Treta age the world became full of rajas, and he says gods are pleased by offerings, not by flesh and blood. A king named Kshatrasimha comes to Mohana, who tells of reciting the Saptashati and the goddess who creates and protects the world, and lists her powers such as Shachi, Siddhi, thirst, contentment, love, conduct, harm and patience. Kshatrasimha is tested by questions. The chapter says this is the time of Vikrama's story, and that a king will restore the holy places. Vetala vanishes and tells the sages, headed by Suta, that twilight has come.

06-023.json.summary: Vyasa tells that the sages lived in deep trance for a year. At that time King Vikramaditya is mentioned. The sages go to Suta and propose to have the king perform a horse sacrifice by his command. Suta comes with them. The horse goes to Kapila's place in the east and the bridge to Lanka in the south, and then to the Kshipra river. All the gods with their wives come to the king's sacrifice. After it the king gives many gifts, together with Vetala, and the moon gives nectar water and vanishes. The king gives the nectar to Indra, who goes to heaven. A Brahmin named Jayanta praises Bhartrihari for a hundred thousand gold pieces, and Vikramaditya rules without thorns. Shaunaka and the sages, knowing the king reached heaven, hear Suta recite the Puranas again.

06-024.json.summary: Vyasa asks Suta for something for people's good across the four ages. Suta begins with a salutation to Rama with Lakshmana and Sita. Once the yogi Narada, wishing to help others, sees the sufferings of people in the Kali age and asks how their sorrow may surely end. He goes to the white, four-armed Narayana, who is calm, cheerful and praised by Sanaka and others. Narada says that duty has four feet with truth as its ornament, and the best means is the Satya Narayana vow, and asks what the fruit and rule are. The Lord says that by it a person bound is freed, a fearful one becomes fearless. One bathes in the morning, is pure, takes a tooth-stick, resolves "I will keep your vow", and worships in the evening, with Shaligrama and gold, and recites the six-chapter story. The offering is divided between the teacher and the family, and Brahmins are fed. Narada then goes to heaven.

06-025.json.summary: Suta tells of the famous city of Kashi and an excellent but poor Brahmin there. Narayana appears to a gentle, humble man and says "by my advice, worship Satya Narayana". The Brahmin, instructed by the kind Hari, praises him with a hymn, describing him in a yellow garment with lotus eyes. The Lord gives the rule: with little effort and simple faith one worships, offering wheat flour with ghee, Ganga water with honey and the five nectars, with sweet food, drink, fruit and honour, surrounded by Brahmins and relatives, and the offering is eaten with respect. The Lord vanishes. The Brahmin and his wife do as told, call relatives and friends, and the Brahmin asks for happiness here and hereafter. He receives a chariot, an elephant, a house and a horse. They bow to the ground and receive the offering, and he spreads the worship of Satya Narayana in the world.

06-026.json.summary: Suta tells of a calm, gentle, wise king devoted to Narayana, Chandrachuda of Manipura, who fights a dreadful battle with proud foreigners. His great army goes to Yama's city, and five thousand footmen die and go to heaven. Overcome by the foreigners, he goes to Kashi on the pretext of a pilgrimage. He sees the city rich in wealth and grain, is amazed, and, seeing the Brahmin Sadananda who worships the true god, bows to him. Sadananda describes the Satya Narayana vow: gateways and plantain pillars, a lovely altar built by Brahmins in the middle, and worship with perfumes and flowers with love and devotion. The king worships in Kashi, takes a sword that destroys the enemy's side, kills six thousand bandits, and gains great wealth. By keeping the vow on every full-moon day, he becomes lord of a hundred thousand villages.

06-027.json.summary: Suta tells that some hunters go to Kashi to sell wood from the forest. They see Hari, served by Brahmins, and a Brahmin once seen as poor now seen as very rich, and ask how he got his wealth. Sadananda tells them of the Satya Narayana worship and the history of how a Nishada came to his hermitage. The rule is: wheat flour with ghee, bathing the god with the five nectars, and worship with sandal and others with fruit, flowers, incense and lamps. Pure devotion pleases him more than many things. He left the honour offered by Duryodhana, and ate the rice grains of Sudama. A cowherd, a vulture, a merchant, a hunter, Hanuman and Vibhishana reached him and are happy still. The hunters sell the wood, worship with the proceeds, bow at the end of the story and take the offering. By the power of the worship they gain children and wives and enjoy pleasures, and the poor and blind are said to gain as they wish.

06-028.json.summary: Suta tells of King Chandrachuda of Manipura and, in the city of Ratnapura, a merchant (Sadhu) who owns a hundred thousand. He sees many people at a river shore, rests his boat to see the wonder, and asks what they are doing. They say the worship of the true god gives wealth, a son, and all wishes. He wishes for a child, goes home thinking of Hari, holds festivals, and then has a lotus-eyed daughter. A daughter is said to be ten years old before she is a young woman. He chooses a fitting groom and gives the daughter with Vedic sound and music. He treats his son-in-law like a son. He then leaves with ships on trade. While all sleep, thieves steal his great wealth. The king hears of the theft, is angry, and has the merchant and son-in-law arrested and chained for twelve months, as the god was hostile. They lament.

06-029.json.summary: Suta continues the merchant's story. When Hari is against one, he says, many hells await. The merchant's wife Kalavati and her daughter, without food or clothing, are in need, and a man, Shilapala, gives five coins. The king is taught by a Brahmin in a dream. The merchant and his son-in-law say they are not thieves, ask to be judged truly, and the minister speaks. They are freed with song and music. Later an ascetic tells the merchant that his wealth is not in the boats, and the merchant faints from worry. The ascetic says that when King Chandrachuda worshipped Satya Narayana, he did not honour him, so how can he prosper? The merchant asks forgiveness and the pleased Narayana grants his wish. Kalavati ignores the offering and hurries away, and her son-in-law sinks with the boat; she faints, and is told to take the offering quickly. By the power of the vow the merchant is blessed with sons and grandsons. This is called the best of vows.

06-030.json.summary: The sages ask Suta about the highest celibate life, and Suta says that in the terrible Kali age, there is no forest-dwelling stage and celibacy is seen only here and there. A man asks what stage and class will do him good, and decides to take a wife, thus praising Shiva, the auspicious one, with a hymn that salutes Nature, the mother of the great principle, who makes the pairs of opposites, and Ignorance and Purity. A Brahmin marries the goddess named Brahmacharini and gives the seasonal gift to his wife. The four Vedas are named. The son of the Yajurveda is the Mimamsa teacher, and Vararuchi, a favourite of the king, is the son of the Atharva Veda. The king honours them. Vyadi, Mimamsa and Panini each speak to Chandragupta, and Vararuchi speaks to the king of Magadha. The student with staff and the almsman is named, and Pitrisharma meditates on Damodara.

06-031.json.summary: Suta tells that Panini, ashamed, goes to other holy places, drinks the water at Kedara and meditates on Shiva. After ten days he lives on air for ten days and, hearing nectar-like words, praises the god with a choking voice: "salutation to Bharga, the destroyer of sin, endless and Creator", and asks him to give the root of knowledge. The god says that the mind is the great holy place in the lake of knowledge, with the water of truth removing the dirt of passion and hatred, which shows Brahman. Then Rudra vanishes and Panini goes home. After composing the Linga-sutra, he attains the highest liberation. The Ganga herself, the auspicious one made of all holy places, comes there.

06-032.json.summary: Suta tells that Bopadeva goes to lovely Vrindavana, served by cowherds and cowherd women, and at the end of a year Hari himself gives him the best knowledge, described by Shuka to the wise Vishnurata. At the end of the story the Lord Vishnu appears. Bopadeva says people tormented by hell are fulfilled through his name in the Kali age. The Lord says the world will be ruled by Buddhists, made of pride and hypocrisy. The goddess Shiva asks who the best god is and, hearing the answer, goes to a secret place where Chandisha, Ganesha, Nandin and Guha are. The god tells her a lovely story kept in his mind. A parrot in a hollow hears it, becomes long-lived, and gains the greatness of the Bhagavata. The goddess is told to go to the bank of the Narmada and recite the story, and to give it to a worthy Vishnu devotee. Bopadeva then vanishes.

06-033.json.summary: The sages ask by which hymn one gains the fruit of reciting the Vedas, and Suta tells a story. A Brahmin named Tripathin has a wife, Kamini. He goes to recite the Saptashati for a living and stays away for a month. She meets a hunter who lives by selling wood and conceives by him. After twelve years the cunning son, who has no Vedic learning, and his mother are driven out by the Brahmin. Living on the Vindhya mountain, they recite the Chandika text daily, and both live happily in a hunter's house in the forest. The son steals, takes a woman's ornaments, and once receives something taken from a Brahmin's clothes, but by the merit of reciting the text he turns to righteousness and becomes a pupil, reciting the letters of Shiva. A worm-like being comes out of him, burnt in many colours. He recites the Adi Charita and praises Annapurna with a hymn. After a hundred and eight recitations the goddess gives him the Rigveda and disappears. He becomes the priest for King Vikramaditya's sacrifice.

06-034.json.summary: Suta tells that a wicked man out of greed for meat ate pigs and village cocks, then human flesh, and gave up everything else. The fearful man has the Chandika recitation done. He becomes a Kshatriya king of Magadha again, remembers his past lives and follows Vedic duty. A sage gives the king the middle episode of the Devi Mahatmya, and the king worships the eternal Mahalakshmi daily. By the grace of Mahamaya the place becomes holy. After twelve years his teacher, devoted to Shakti, arrives, and the eternal goddess, mother of the world, appears. The king, great and fortunate, enjoys pleasures the gods desire. Suta says this is the fate of the Yajurveda as told, and the greatness described by the sage.

06-035.json.summary: Suta tells of a man who knows the Vedas and their branches and is devoted to the Gita. Once he goes on a pilgrimage, and at the end of the year he is won over by a devotee of the goddess. Patanjali praises her: "you are faith, understanding, memory, learning, and the one who does good". A disembodied voice says he will gain true knowledge by the power of her story. He goes to the temple of Vindhyavasini and gains the knowledge that is her grace and turns to Vishnu. He wears the upright mark, tilaka and a tulasi necklace, and recites the Mahabhashya joyfully to each person. Suta says this is the best prayer to recite and ends with a blessing: may all see good and none share in sorrow. The listener who is pure and hears the collection of histories is blessed.

07-001.json.summary: This chapter begins the fourth part of the Pratisarga. The sages ask about the play the Lord performed at that time. Suta says that in the great kalpa called Bhavishya, in the Vaivasvata age, the Pandavas defeated the proud Kauravas. At the end of a day Krishna, knowing the bad turn of time, asks Shiva to protect the Pandavas who are his devotees. At night Ashvatthama, Bhoja and Kripa come, and Ashvatthama kills with a sword given by Shiva. A charioteer of Dhrishtadyumna survives, frightened. Learning that Shiva has done wrong, Bhima and the others become angry and their weapons enter Shiva's body. Rudra curses them: "you are worshippers of Krishna and will be reborn in the Kali age and bear this fault". They take refuge in Hari and praise Rudra, and Shiva appears. Krishna says he gave the curse out of necessity and tells who will be born: Yudhishthira as Vatsaraja's son, Bhima as a foreigner, a part of Arjuna as a devotee, Nakula at Kanyakubja, Sahadeva, a part of Dhritarashtra at Ajmer, and Karna as Taraka. Mahavati is a lovely city made by Mayadevi, and a part of Krishna is born as Udayasimha. He says he will kill the kings of the fire line and establish Kali.

07-002.json.summary: Suta describes kings who taught the duties of kings, liberation and giving, and went to heaven after ruling thirty-six years. Vyasa says the sages of Naimisha, after twelve hundred years, rise at a divine pool and do bathing and meditation. They name the lands, from the west end of the Sindhu river to Setubandha in the south, Ajmer, Marudhanva, Avanti, Udupa, Vanga, Gauda and Magadha, where many languages and religions stand. Hearing of the ruin of duty, they come with many groups by the Himalaya and Sindhu routes. A grandson of Vikramaditya takes his father's kingdom, sets a boundary between the foreigners and Aryas, and makes a foreign settlement beyond the Sindhu. In the middle of the Huna country, a good man on a mountain tells the king that he teaches the foreigners' way, and that a fearful being called Ishamasi appeared among bandits at the decline of truth. He tells the king to recite a pure Vedic prayer and meditate on the Lord in the sun's disc. The king bows, regains his kingdom and performs a horse sacrifice.

07-003.json.summary: Suta tells that the limits of duty were slowly lost on earth. A king with ten thousand soldiers and Kalidasa conquers the foreigners of Gandhara, Kashmir and Narava. Another foreigner comes with a teacher, and King Bhoja prays to Mahadeva, "lord of Girija, dweller in the desert, hidden by foreigners, pure and of the form of being, consciousness and bliss". The land of Bahlika is polluted by foreigners, with a great magician whom the god had burnt earlier. The god tells the king not to go to the demon-like land. The king returns home. A man skilled in magic speaks to him lovingly and tells him to eat his leftovers. The king's mind turns to the foreign way. Kalidasa, angry, says he will kill the wicked Bahlika, recites ten thousand times and makes the fire offering. The frightened disciples go to Bahlika. At night a god-like man tells the king that his Aryan way is the best. He says those who are circumcised, shaveless, bearded and defile are different, and that animals should be eaten except by the Kaula rite. The king returns home and sets up the Prakrit language for Shudras and a boundary for the foreigners. People of Aryan classes stay beyond the Vindhyas, and mixed castes live in Barbara, Tushara and many islands.

07-004.json.summary: Suta says the earth had many kings in their kingdom, and three kings of their line died within two hundred years. The king ruled his own kingdom by duty at Kalpakshetra. In Indraprastha Anangapala of the Tomara family is named. The fire line grew stronger, from the north to the end of China and to Setubandha in the south, with fire-offering makers who care for cows and Brahmins. A time like the Dvapara age returns everywhere, with a god and a sacrifice in every village and land. Seeing this, the terrible Kali, afraid with Mleccha, practised meditation for twelve years. Kali praises Hari, who removes all sin and makes all time, saying he has lost his body, family and kingdom. Krishna, laughing, says a part of him will come to earth and destroy the mighty ones, and vanishes. A king keeps the nine-night Durga vow for nine years, and the goddess grants a boon. He marries by duty and settles her at home. Acharya, Vatsaraja, a foreigner called Shatayatta and the mighty Talana are named. A battle of the two kings is dreadful, and then they make friendship with Talana.

07-005.json.summary: Suta tells of the birth of two girls by Shiva's favour, for King Someshvara of the Chauhan family. A Brahmin, Jayasharma, is in trance on the Himalaya, gives up his body, and a part of Nakula is born on earth by Shiva's command. He conquers Gauda, Vanga and others and the proud desert lands. Three proud sons are born to Kirtimalini, and Simhakhela at twelve years. Dhundhukara rules at Mathura and his younger brother at Ajmer. A strong son of Pradyota named Parimala is born, and Bhishmasimha, lord of elephants, from Vidyota. Seeing those unfriendly to him, he drives them from his kingdom. A bold son who gained his maternal grandfather's kingdom is told by those he has driven out how he can enjoy all the kingdom. King Jayachandra says "Parimala, you are brave, be my minister now". They are glad. A fort city is built, and Delhi is founded at a good time at the fort's gate, and the king, amazed, names it Delhi. After three years Jayachandra asks Prithviraj why he did not give his share, and sends a messenger. A proud king says he drove out the cunning men of the moon line and gathered sixteen hundred thousand troops, and that the strong king must pay tax. Jayachandra, afraid of Prithviraj, is shown, and Prithviraj takes half the kingdom.

07-006.json.summary: Suta tells that Mahiraja (Prithviraj) is amazed at the news. A woman named Tilaka is named. A Gauda king's daughter, Divyavibhavari, has a daughter, Samyogini. At Kanyakubja a golden image of Kamakshi is set up. The goddess says to a father that if he worships this yogini she will be dear to him. Five thousand chariots with archers, Dhundhukara, lord of elephants, and eight hundred thousand horses are named. The army stretches twenty krosha. On the far bank of the Ishani river, a palanquin is placed. Pradyota and Vidyota guard Ratnabhanu. Horses die by horses and elephants by elephants. The battle lasts five days with great loss of heroes. A hundred thousand horses die and go to heaven. Dhundhukara strikes Pradyota in the heart with arrows, three spears fell him to the ground, and a spear kills him and he goes to heaven. Lakshana, with them, fights angrily. The two equal heroes fight on elephants. When the mighty one is killed, the people of Kanyakubja flee in fear of Mahiraja, to their homes. Prithviraj wins, and Jayachandra's fame in battle is told. Jayachandra rules at Kanyakubja and Prithviraj at Delhi.

07-007.json.summary: Suta tells that Bhishmasimha, on the Ganga's bank in the sign of Leo, worships Indra, and after a month Indra, knowing his devotion, gives him gifts and vanishes. At that time Parimala, grieving for his father, goes to Kashi to die with his wife. A serpent at a root tells the Rudra serpent that he is cruel and slow-witted, and he has been glad in the king's body every day. A fool king, it says, is the one who does not give hot oil. The king does what the serpent said and is freed of disease. At midnight in the darkness, a sun appears in all directions, and he praises Shiva with the Mahimna hymn. Mahadeva takes the form of a linga. Malkhana, pleased, comes to Mahavati and goes to Jayachandra's city after a year. Lakshana, a hero, prays to the lord of Usha. Within a fortnight Vishnu, the lord of the world, answers, and Lakshana goes home on the elephant Airavati. They live together in friendship. A group says they will go to their cities, and the king agrees. Karinari, Sulalita and others are named. Talana is a hero at his son's command, dear to Rakshasas, and two sons of Vasuman are named. The king is given a five-voiced great serpent from Indra and a horse, Papiha, a gift of the sun, with a human voice. The army is sixty thousand, with Talana as its lord. Protected by these heroes the king is fulfilled.

07-008.json.summary: Suta tells how a king worships Shiva with earth images, and the god offers a boon, which the king asks for with folded hands. Mahadeva grants it and vanishes. A strong man, going to deliver a message, says he will go with the troops to the pure Ganga, and speaks to his sister, who wants victory; she gives a jewelled necklace. Kaliya comes quickly with a hundred thousand horses. After giving gifts to Brahmins he goes to Jayachandra's city. A strong man who got a boon from Shiva goes to lovely Mahavati and takes refuge in Rudra, Shambhu with matted hair. A great battle lasting a day and night follows with Vatsaraja, who has sixteen thousand horses, and the heroes of both armies fall. They destroy the enemy army and cry out in victory. Kaliya is defeated, Bhishmasimha rouses the soldiers and strikes an enemy with an arrow named Bhairava, the army of Mahishmati scatters in ten directions, and a king cuts off his head. King Parimala and Jayachandra are amazed at the enemy's defeat. Five months after Bhishmasimha's death, a part of Sahadeva is born on earth by Shiva's command, and the king gives much wealth at the news.

07-009.json.summary: Suta tells of a thousand-fold Chandika fire offering and a meeting of many kings. Two heroes had been bound each day by the king's daughters. Devaki is given to Desharaja and Brahmi to his younger brother, with a hundred elephants, five chariots, a thousand horses, servants and much wealth. When a son is born, Devaki conceives again. The baby is known as a part of Rama, with a cheerful face. A month later Brahmi bears a son, and the Brahmins, seeing him, are glad. At three years Balakhani is born, and Chamunda, Devaki's son, is named as a danger to his own line. Jambuka comes with his troops against Vatsaraja, and a great battle with seven hundred thousand men of Mahishmati follows. By Shiva's boon, the brothers are defeated. The enemy burns the whole city and goes home. A goddess's favourite carries a seven-month part of Krishna and, in the land of Kalpa, sets him in the Yamuna. On the eighth of the dark fortnight of Bhadrapada, the dark-limbed, lotus-eyed boy shining like a sapphire is born, and a voice from the sky says that Udaya has been born as the sun among gods. Brahmi bears a strong son, a part of an attendant. The children grow, and at three years the strong part of Krishna and the divine mare Ashvini and Harini near Uchchaihshravas are mentioned. At eight Krishna's part does the name ceremony.

07-010.json.summary: Suta tells how the code of duty became the best of all. A king sends his army to Mahavati for tribute, and the people there are told to give a sixth as a tax to the king. The king hears and sends a lakh of heroes to Kanyakubja. Many local rulers are in his land, and Mahiraja, hearing this, is greatly afraid. The son of the lord of Urvi, a strong sixteen-year-old, is mentioned, and a king speaks lovingly to his nephew, asking him to wrestle. Astrologers are called and the time asked. The northern Naimisharanya becomes his own country. Hearing this, Krishna's part is hurt by words like arrows. Seeing his son faint, the king takes a sword in hand, and another king stops him. The boy bows to the father. The chapter then tells of the mare Harini and the gift of Indra to Bhishmasimha. The sages ask about Harini, and Suta tells the earlier story: King Desharaja, a pious man, asks a boon, and from that union horses are born. Harini gives birth to Megha and Pushpa and Balahaka. A tiger, terror of beings, is killed by Ahlada. The goddess Sharada, fair-faced, is mentioned, and says "remember me when you are afraid" and vanishes. The king sees their valour and is glad.

07-011.json.summary: Suta tells that the heroes stay in a vow in the month of Madhava, worshipping with seasonal flowers, incense and lamps. The goddess gives a boon, and they go home, their purpose achieved. In Ashadha, Krishna's part, riding a horse, gives gold to the twice-born. At the king's order warriors try to bind him, but the hero is awakened by divine illusion. Women, seeing his lovely form, try to charm him. Hearing a piteous word, he leaves his city. When Krishna's part is eleven and fierce in battle, his sister sees her brother distressed and tells him something, calling Dhundhukara. Devasimha, who knows the time, hears the enemy is coming and says he will deal with Mahiraja and Dhundhukara with their troops. The enemy arrive with four hundred thousand soldiers and make a loud noise. Sixty thousand of the army go to heaven. Horses fight horses and camels fight camel riders. Brahmananda sends enemies to Yama's house with arrows. Seeing his army beaten, the strong Dhundhukara is wounded on an elephant and faints. A strong man, with a boon from Shiva, comes riding an elephant, worships his guns and makes a great slaughter. He makes Mahiraja and his relatives with their mounts faint and binds Sukhakhani and others in strong chains. Balakhani goes by Devasimha's order. King Parimala comes gladly and returns home with Brahmananda.

07-012.json.summary: Suta tells how at lovely Kanyakubja many kings come together with armies. Jambuka, a king with the people of the Narmada, is named. Krishna's part speaks quickly to his mother. Talana comes quickly with four hundred thousand troops. Flags of five thousand and a thousand woodcutters are mentioned. They bow to King Malana and give many gifts. Seeing his mother deluded, they are glad. Krishna's part speaks softly to a woman, dances, and Balakhani sings. A courtesan, learning her son Ahlada has become a yogi, sees the heroes bound and shuts a door to bind them. The two armies meet to fight. Seeing his army broken, Kaliya goes to Balakhani, and Suryavarman, learning his relative Kaliya is bound, comes. The great battle lasts many days with heroes of Mahishmati and Rankana. Talana is the angry commander every day. A woman skilled in illusion goes to comfort her father, and uses a Rakshasi's illusion. A prince who was a great demon named Chitra in a past life is named. King Jambuka, with a boon from Shiva, is bound with strong iron chains. The goddess Devaki, devoted to her husband, kills the enemy's sons, and orders Jambuka's body crushed with oils she has made. All the soldiers return to Mahavati, joyful and fulfilled.

07-013.json.summary: The sages ask, and Suta tells that a king offers wealth of half a crore. Krishna's part sits on Bindula and Vatsaja on Harini. At the full moon when Rahu seizes the moon in darkness, he gives the nectar-drum to the king and speaks again. Netrasimha, who looked after him like a son, is named. Two friends come in palanquins to the king. A woman worships Durga and recites the middle episode of the Chandi. A man goes to the flower-garden in Mahavati. A man says his father, enemy by Indra's boon, is such. On the fifth of the dark fortnight of Magha, he tells him to come quickly with signs of battle on his body. He speaks to the mighty king Netrasimha, who faints with anger. Netrasimha with kings of the hills fights a dreadful battle. Krishna's part, on a divine horse, comforts them. He worships the giver of all wishes with the music of the nectar-drum. A father says he has seen the same in a dream. The maiden is meant for a famous part of Rama. The enemy are told that they are Aryan Abhiras and that they will perish with their families like Jambuka. A thousand kings are placed in a tent with their forces. Sukhakhani blocks the victory at the third turn. Balakhani takes Harini, Harinagara is mentioned, and Netrasimha, the fine brother, king of Sundara forest. Messengers on camels bring news, and King Malana holds a great festival in every house.

07-014.json.summary: Suta says that on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra, at noon on a Thursday, a best of sons is born, and the gods with sages come. Ahlada, gladly, has the birth rites for the child performed. Indula is born as a son, and after two months a hundred troops of dancers with songs are mentioned on earth. Yogasimha stays seven nights and goes home. Out of love for the boy he takes him away by his magic, and Shachi gives the child her own breast. The moon takes the house of nectar in his own body. When the child is lost, Goddess Svarnavati and Ahlada learn what happened in the ten villages, and Ahlada with his family fasts and controls his senses. The pleased goddess speaks as a disembodied voice: Jayanta, Indra's son, has gone to heaven. As long as Ahlada stayed on earth, the boy would stay on earth. Hearing this, they were free of grief.

07-015.json.summary: Suta tells that after reciting the Saptashati at the three twilights with love and devotion, a Brahmin's son named Chamunda, born to Samanta, grew famous. At twelve, after reading the three-part text, he says he will fill a vessel for devotees. Sukhakhani brings honey, flowers and fruit, and Devaki honours the goddess with offerings and sandal. Ahlada bows with his whole body and Udaya with his head. The goddess, loving her devotees, speaks to them. She says the great hero Balakhani will die after a long time, Devaki will be a goddess and go to her own world for a long time, and Devasimha, free of desire, will gain liberation when he dies.

07-016.json.summary: Suta tells that when King Ratnabhanu dies, the king of Marudhanva comes. The Lord is pleased and gives a fine horse, Pavakiya, a horse of fire. The men are eighteen years old. On the eighth of the bright fortnight of Margashirsha on a Monday, Gajamukta sees the hero and is enchanted. Seeing Balakhani attacked on all sides, Taraka comes. When the king's army is beaten, the strong Balakhani is bound with iron chains. The fierce men bind and beat him. The king, knowing the cause, with his hands tied, says that his daughter has come to the house and that he is lucky to be alive. A wedding for Balakhani is mentioned, and he is asked to come with his troops. Balakhani ate poison but did not die, by a good boon. Gajamukta comes. Hearing the terrible words, he grieves. Seeing her husband in such a state, Gajamukta is very sad. Ahlada with seven hundred thousand troops fights a battle of a day and night. Seeing the army burnt to ashes, Talana faces the enemy. Knowing his brother is tied, Kantamala mounts a horse. Half of Gajasena's army is destroyed. By the goddess's word, Indula by Indra's command comes, and the fire is calmed. Some became ascetics, some students. Balakhani is driven out, then Talana. They stay in iron forts at night. The fearful king with his two daughters hears this. When Ahlada reaches home, the goddess Svarnavati herself comes. Indula bows to his mother. King Parimala, wise, hears of Ahlada's return.

07-017.json.summary: Suta tells that Mahiraja, greatly grieved, has the Lakshachandi rite performed. Seven sons will be born every year from his body. Saradana, part of Uddharsha, and Mardana, part of Durmukha, are named. When a girl is born on earth, a dreadful earthquake happens. Ila, mother of the moon, is born on earth by choice. A voice says that whoever bathes the speaker with streams of blood in the hall will win. A man takes three hundred thousand in wealth and a hundred thousand soldiers. Brahmananda, strong, says he will go. Hearing this, Taraka goes quickly with his forces, and all fall silent. Lakshana with Talana and seven hundred thousand troops come. The one who commands twelve hundred thousand troops is strong. Krishna, sitting on Bindula, is mentioned. Ranajit, Malana's son, stays at Harinagara. Five thousand carts and buffalo-drawn vehicles are named. At the fort gate, a good rite is done. Ahlada goes himself and gives an ornament to Vela. Nrihari goes against Krishna's part a second time. A hundred sword-bearing kings and Gajasena and others are mentioned. Remembering Shiva, he wins and binds in anger. Krishna's part, unbeaten, goes through the sky to the temple. He takes a palanquin and reaches the camp himself. After the wedding they all come to the camps. He kills a thousand warriors and binds the strong again. A man speaks to Pradyota's son, saying Lakshana is strong. Mahiraja takes the king's feet. He is told to leave her and go home happy. Malana sees his son married at home. Lakshana speaks at the assembly at the time of departure.

07-018.json.summary: Suta tells that swans come down from the sky and speak to Indula, calling him blessed with a divine body and saying Mahavati is the ocean among cities. They tell him they saw a lovely woman decked with ornaments on a lake and were enchanted. They ask him to ride them and see her. In the lovely land of Simhala, King Aryasimha lives, and a Gauri temple stands by a lotus lake. The woman sees Indula, handsome, in the form of a swan, and he stays a year, charmed by many sports. When Ahlada, the elder, grows proud of devotion, the goddess sends him great sorrow. The people of Lanka hear of Indula. The family weeps at the news. Krishna's part, weeping, speaks to Ahlada, and Balakhani, Devasimha and Talana set out. They defeat proud kings on the road, worship Shiva Rameshvara, set up by Rama, and reach the lotus lake. They ask Aryasimha to give them boats to cross. Indula fixes a stunning mantra on an arrow. For six months the two armies fight.

07-019.json.summary: Suta tells that Devasimha, who knows the three times, is called, and a son of Indra, skilled in weapons, is mentioned. The heroes mount horses and Krishna's part enters the king's inner palace. When the mighty hero (Balakhani, with Devasimha and Talana) is killed, Jayanta faints in anger. He goes home amazed. He goes to Aryasimha's house and asks the cause of everything. Someone weeps on a mare, crying for the great hero Indula. Indra's strong son arrives and says victory will not come by destroying the army. When Indula faints, a divine mare appears. With the commander dead, Krishna's part, delirious, by his own yoga drinks a fine wind weapon, and again by the power of yoga that weapon is destroyed. At dawn the strong Balakhani says he will take his head with his own sword. The child, knowing his family, speaks sweetly to a dear one and weeps out of love. Aryasimha with much wealth sends them off with a voice choked with love. Ahlada, glad, receives his son with his wife. Prithviraj is astonished at the news. A heavenly nymph gave up her state and became a woman on earth, and after dying of wasting disease went to heaven.

07-020.json.summary: Suta tells of a king of the Bisena line, skilled in the truth of the Vedas, with two sons devoted to warrior duty. One of them lives as a silent forest-dweller with self-control. The commander of the gods, Skanda, born of fire, is pleased. Mayuradhvaja praises him: "victory to your divine body, that leads groups of gods". The king speaks humbly and names a city, Mayuranagara, full of people. His brother Lahara tries for twenty years. Hearing the nectar-like words, King Lahara speaks, praising the god. By his grace the king gets a lovely queen, and sixteen sons. Devasimha, taken as the best of the moon line, bows to King Parimala. A strong man asks his uncle with humility. After being begged by many Brahmins, the king goes home. A Shudra bridegroom is warned against as mixing the castes. King Jambuka and King Netrasimha are said to be conquered. On the tenth of the bright fortnight of Magha, Balakhani and the others go to battle at the king's command, are defeated, and a few return afraid. Their bows are cut and they are bound. When the army has become like water, the strong Jayanta comes. Varuna, lord of waters, appears. The parts accept a great worship given by Lahara. This is the account of Krishna's part.

07-021.json.summary: A sage tells that Krishna's part, with Devasimha, worships and is glad. A gardener's daughter tells the king how Makaranda came to be. Makaranda becomes strong at five. A lovely divine grove worshipped by gods is described. At the end of the month the king is told everything at home. Krishna's part prays to the goddess, Devamaya, Mahamaya, the one ever pure, who burnt Dhumralochana and destroyed Chanda and Munda. In the rainy season of four months, a lovely necklace is strung by Krishna's part. Someone asks for life and says she will tell the reason. Makaranda's fear is said to hold gods and men on earth. Pushpavati, the dutiful one, speaks again. Daily a garland is made for worship. She has seen a lovely young woman. When her palanquin reaches the fort door, he tells her to come to his house, as she is now his wife. He seizes her by force and touches her heart. The city of Mahavati is described. Hearing the news, King Makaranda gathers five thousand guns, ten thousand elephants and a hundred thousand horses. A fierce battle lasts day and night. The son of the fire fights on a stone horse that protects him, but Brahmananda comes with a hundred thousand and Mayuradhvaja is also named. By the power of a Vishnu weapon, the stone horse becomes ashes. A daughter is given by rule with much wealth.

07-022.json.summary: A narrator tells that Krishna's strong part arrives at Mahavati and spends cold seasons in private play with Pushpavati, who is skilled in song and dance. He says he was King Chandradasa in an earlier life, and at the day of his death his mind was on the Shaligrama stone. He says whenever duty declines, the Lord appears, and sages, gods and ancestors welcome it. Pushpavati says that in a past birth she was a courtesan, Chandrakanti. Kali begged the god, her lord, for his own sake, and by his order she was born as Jambuka's daughter. Her husband's brother was tormented because of that fault. The king, learning the cause, sends the letter written by Malana. Kamasena, Prasena and Mahasena are named. A boy of twenty is forgotten by his parents. Udaya speaks humbly to his sister. They went again to Simhala for Jayanta. King Virasena learns the true cause and gives food to Chandravali. A man takes him by the arms to bind him. Udaya kills a hundred thousand great warriors, riding Bindula. Virasena binds him, frees the sons and the bride, and the king is told to release his brother-in-law. When a weapon is readied, the strong Brahmananda with Krishna's part comes. Malana, seeing his son, trembles with love.

07-023.json.summary: Suta tells of Brahmins fed and given fees. A magical vessel in mid-Ganga is mentioned. Krishna's part awakens and does not see his child. His brother Udaya, intoxicated, bewitches the two. His mother, wife and sister grieve with love. A man says to tear out his eyes and show him. The hero, with permission from Gajamukta, finds the couple and goes fearlessly. A land hard to reach, with enemies turning to stone, is described. The god speaks and vanishes, and the king is amazed. A man says he will do his work quickly and give back the son. Chitrarekha, her mind shaken by grief, says "give me the parrot, Mahamaya, or Indula". A letter written by Indula is taken. A man speaks humbly to King Mahipati. Brahmananda arrives with three hundred thousand troops. One chariot stands in the war, with elephants behind. King Abhinandana's foreigners follow the ghoul's way. Seeing the army's ruin, the king's seven sons come. Suryavarman fights Upananda and Taraka fights Sunanda. The actress Keshari binds eight warriors. A couple at Makaranda's house are seen. A man cuts the illusion of Shambara and wakes his soldiers. Svarnavati kills the wonder. Pranandha, Virasena and Brahmananda are named. Cries of "O Krishna's part, mighty-armed refuge of those who come to you" are heard. The yogi, Krishna's part, a portion of the Lord, appears, and tells his story. He sends off the great Balakhani. All the kings, honoured by Ahlada, go home.

07-024.json.summary: Suta tells that Taraka, having told the king the news, receives good knowledge from her that destroys wrong thoughts. Four divine horses, which go on water, land and sky, are named, and a man is told to give back the horses she called. A promise is made on life. Devaki, full of grief, hears the oath. Indula goes quickly with ten thousand horse troops. Devasimha, blunted, goes to Krishna's part. An arrow driven by a Vishnu mantra fails. Lakshana speaks and goes with him to King Jayachandra. Seeing the horses Kuvalayapida die, the king is afraid. In a few hours the strong man wins and takes tribute of sixteen years, then twenty years, a crore of gold. Lakshana goes to the Pundra country. The heroes go to Virasimhapura and fight for half a month. Krishna's part and the others take a form of yoga, and praise a god, saying they will bow if a boon is given. The yogi vanishes. On the lovely day of Holika, Lakshana attacks. A father says: "son, always do the king's work, fond of war". If you beat Balakhani and give him to me. His younger brother Sukhakhani with troops comes. At dawn, after bathing, they go. Balakhani is surrounded by the proud heroes. A fine fire arrow that destroys enemies is mentioned. Seeing Chamunda in a woman's dress, the king hears this. Messengers go to Delhi, and Mahiraja turns to Mahadeva.

07-025.json.summary: Suta tells what happened when Krishna's part was twenty-six. A village a league wide stands on a river bank. A king of Vishvaksena's line lives there and worships the Prajapati with sacrifices. A lovely daughter reaches twelve. Kings come from many lands with chief warriors. He places his own army to protect all the kings. A man of forty or fifty is named. Lakshana takes her excellent hand. Ahlada rides a five-voiced elephant with a Tomara weapon. The god rides Manoratha and fits a Bhairava spear. The fight lasts an hour. Mahiraja says Lakshana is without duty and mixes the castes. By the goddess's boon, Devasimha at night does something. Padmakara uses the Shambara illusion. The strong ones wake with the love weapon. Sharadanandana bows to them, gives his daughter, who weeps, then cows, clothes and ornaments. He goes with seven hundred thousand to Shirisha city. With a fire weapon he kills ten thousand. Mahiraja takes up a fierce weapon, takes revenge for his brother, and kills the enemy's army. A man says he made twelve pits at a distance of a krosha. Chamunda comes with ten thousand arrows. A thirteenth hidden pit is covered with grass and earth, and Vatsaja's lotus foot is torn. Gajamukta puts her husband on the pyre. Brahma comes with his wife. The king turns the empty city to ashes.

07-026.json.summary: Suta tells of a festival of Nagas with song and dance. Mahipati bows to a king of the moon line. Hearing this, King Parimala is led by fate. A hymn is addressed to the great goddess who removes all sorrow, and the goddess Sharada goes to Krishna's part. Hearing it, he goes with Lakshana. A battle of a week, increasing death, follows. Yadava on an elephant, husband of Chandravali, appears. Chamunda leads ten thousand troops. Malana, seeing his brother, speaks in grief. A Brahmin, tormented by the fire of passion, is Chamunda. Brahma and others are defeated by them. A yogi Himada is killed by Mahiraja. Balakhani, who goes with ghosts, is addressed. With the sound of a flute Krishna's part dances, charming people. He sees Malana, loving. Her faithful daughter hears. The proud heroes reach Kirtisagara. Brahmananda hears the terrible news. Lakshana and Devasimha and the fearless warrior are named. The yogi army scatters in all directions. Krishna's part goes through the sky. Nrihara, Abhaya, Mardana and Rupana are named. "You are the son of Mahiraja's aunt." Rupana makes Mardana faint, and when Nrihara dies, Mardana is furious. Ranajit, Malana's son, strikes the enemy's neck. Mahiraja, grieving for his son, comes with eight hundred thousand. Dhundhukara goes quickly to Delhi.

07-027.json.summary: Suta tells that someone from the Kachchhapa country of the Gautama line speaks to Malana, saying the lord will not come. "O part of Rama, mighty-armed, handsome child, part of Krishna!" A union of two produced this son, a leader of people. Once Mahiraja with his army stays and makes a settlement named after himself. The hero takes a sword. A man says "you are a Kshatriya who gives livelihood to a Brahmin". Vamana learns the cause from his own messengers. A king is feared by Kshatriyas. Afraid, he gives Harinagara. A hero goes to Kanyakubja. The king is told to come with his army with Ahlada and the others. Jayachandra calls the leader of people. Krishna's part speaks humbly. Jayachandra speaks. The hero with his family and Lakshana cross the Yamuna and reach Kalpakshetra. Chamunda, with a hundred thousand troops, appears. Some heroes die, some are defeated. Lakshana quickly strikes the enemy with his spear. Ahlada and others fear Raktabija. Goddess Devaki speaks to a loving king. After five days Mahiraja comes. When his head is cut, they become heroes of a hundred thousand. Krishna's part praises Sharada, who lives in Brahma's world and takes the form of Chamunda to destroy Raktabija. The king gets a great fear from Mahiraja's words. Prithviraj, in a Brahmin's form, is told. In Phalguna all go home. Balakhani's Gaya rite is done.

07-028.json.summary: Suta tells that Krishna's part, with ten thousand troops and Svarnavati, goes with Pushpavati to a place, and she sees him as the best of men. Learned scholars hear his words and answer a question about the eighteen Puranas: who told them and what they give. Matsya, Kurma, Narasimha, Vamana and Shiva are named, and six Puranas are called "dark" by the wise, devoted to the duty of Shakti. The sages of Naimisha come. A mad woman, Shobha, becomes a beggar. A courtesan, grieving, brings her best ornaments and tells of a pill she has made. She sees the hero, who stirs love, and speaks of her brother Sahara, dear as life. Krishna's part, kind, speaks pitying words, and the hero gives her that wealth. He sees the goddess, mother of the world, in that state. The courtesan takes a lovely body again. A line is spoken about a man who does not approach his married wife at her season. Krishna's part says the sin was cut by austerity, and tells her not to speak the Yavana language even with the breath in her throat. Hearing this, the woman, who is part of a foreigner, takes the form of a hawk and tries to leave. She says she does not know where to go without her husband. The pleased Lord speaks to his servant. Indula and Ahlada are awakened by Vishnu's illusion. They see a Bhairavi illusion that spreads darkness, and the Kshatriyas are deluded and charmed by a dance. Tigers, lions, boars, monkeys, biting insects and men are born from her, and mighty Sharabhas and Tarkshyas. Sahura is crushed by Ahlada with the dancers. The war lasted four months.

07-029.json.summary: The sages ask, and Suta tells of Manjughosha, a heavenly courtesan who comes to the place of Shuka. Shuka, the lord, speaks a lovely verse of praise. He gives her to someone as a wife, the daughter of Svarnadeva. Pleased, Shankara, benefactor of the world, speaks. A king, Bauddhasimha, with seven hundred thousand troops, is mighty. They fight and destroy the enemy army protected by him. At Netrapala's order, Krishna's part and the others come. Talana comes sitting on a lioness. Netrasimha with seven hundred thousand troops, and the others, reach the river Huha. Krishna's part with a hundred thousand, the god with a hundred thousand and the leader of people with a hundred thousand stand ready. Seven hundred thousand Buddhists and two hundred thousand from the Aryan land are killed. A hundred thousand horsemen, wood-carriers and camels, seven thousand of them with brave men, are named. Jayanta, skilled in war, sees the wonder. The Buddhists from China send twenty thousand, and five thousand die, struck by Yogasimha's arrows. Bauddhasimha sends a tiger. A good arrow named Sammohana is taken. All are glad and go to the city. Ten crores of gold go to Ahlada. A hymn praises the king of the gods. Indula, sad, turns to Sharada. The march of the eight strong men is arranged.

07-030.json.summary: Suta tells King Jayachandra to listen carefully. Mahiraja, strong, learns that he comes with his army. Padmakara, Mahiraja's brother-in-law, learns that Lakshana has come, and tells the king that his great enemy Lakshana has come to his house. The goddess, the giver of boons, is pleased. Talana, joined with two others, goes to Kanyakubja. The king, pleased, wears a pearl garland. All the women come, and one weeps and says her husband Lakshana is strong. Hearing it, the king raises his arm. The yogis reach Mahavati. The wise minister Chandrabhatta says he will go to Delhi to ruin the fire line. A woman, Padmini, is called his sister and skilled in hidden arts. Prithviraj takes many ornaments. Kamapala hears that Krishna's part is coming. Svarnavati with her maid Shobha speaks. Ahlada on an elephant and Indula on a fierce horse go to a village, and a man says he was put in an earth pit by Kalagni Rudra. The goddess Svarnavati worships Chandika and comforts them. The woman Padmini prays to Shiva, who speaks after a hundred years. Hearing this, Svarnavati goes to Padmini. Krishna's part, with twelve hundred thousand troops, learns of it. Two vanish and cut the enemy's army with swords. A man bound fearlessly takes Lakshana. Jayachandra sees his own wife and husband at home. This is the account of Krishna's part.

07-031.json.summary: Suta tells that seeing him come, the grieving king speaks. A steady minister tells the king that his son Brahmananda, strong, is with him. By his mother's order, Brahmananda goes with his maternal uncle. Hearing the women's words, he puts on ornaments. A verse says that one who enjoys another's wife goes to Yama's house. Names such as Matta, Pramatta, Unmatta, Sumatta and Durmada are listed. Mahiraja, strong, commands sixteen hundred thousand troops. Hearing, he comes with his whole army, and the battle lasts a day and night. The kind sons of Vatsaja reach Karabha. The Gandharva Sukala is named with his daughter. Krishna's part and others are woken and he returns with them. Nagavarman comes to Mahiraja. Sukhakhani on Papiha and Balakhani on Kapota are named. A king of the Nagas wakes. Madrakesha, who was in the Madra country, has ten sons by boon. Krishna's part goes to the Sahya mountain, to Karbura. The king gives a crore of gold to the great Krishna's part. By the order of the demon Bali, they come to Kurukshetra and kill thousands of demons and reach Bali. Bhumiraja, pleased, gives a crore of gold. Five ten-thousands of heroes flee in fear. A trident is thrust in the enemy's belly by deceit. Vela, hearing this, quickly gets into a palanquin. Two mount and go east near Kapila's. They are told to worship the one who gives all blessings. A man says after killing Taraka he will come to him.

07-032.json.summary: Suta tells of a long series of battles. Krishna's part and others arrive, and Mahiraja has a letter read by the rule. Warriors such as Durmarshana, Dushkarna, Somakirti and Anudara are named as Kauravas of a former birth who bear those names on earth, along with Anadhrishti and Kundabhedi. A king of the Shukla line named Mulavarman comes. Virasena comes with Kamasena and has a hundred thousand and a son. Parimala goes to Mayuradhvaja. The rest are Shudras devoted to heroic acts. At dawn on a dreadful third lunar day, a man says "you with ten brave sons and a hundred thousand troops". Someone cuts Bindula's limb with his own sword. They stay the night, and the leader of the people rises in the morning for battle. A king speaks of the Kinnaras, mighty and his enemies. Remembering Mahendra and Kanaka, he binds and comes to Krishna's part. In three watches, all the warriors on both sides are killed. A man lifts his son and wife, who is weeping. A man says "O Mulavarman of Gurjara, with your sons". Lakshana rises into a chariot against the enemy of his father. Rudravarman with ten thousand warriors is named. In the evening, Lakshana on a female elephant, and Mahiraja, filled with joy, are mentioned. After a night watch, Mahiraja grieves and meditates on Rudra, Maheshvara. Kali with his wife comes. The part of Rama mounts an elephant quickly. A voice says "go, hero, with the troops, you are guarded by me at night". The foreigner Sahoddina makes a binding, takes Vidyunmala and much wealth.

08-001.json.summary: This chapter begins the next part, spoken by Vedavyasa about the Vetala-formed story told again at Vishala, and what he has told, which gives merit. The sages of Naimisha will come to Suta. Suta says the end of Vikrama's tale is followed by a descent of a part of Hari. The sages show great curiosity about four born of fire. A strong king devoted to the Sama Veda lives somewhere. When the strong Buddhist king Ashoka is killed, the sun gladly gives a boon in five years. A strong man brings cowherds and bandits under control. King Gandharvasena, son of a divine messenger, is strong. Shalivahana, son of a devotee of gods, Shalihotra, who ruled fifty years, and Havirhotra are named, each ruling like his father. A king builds the city Indravati and rules there, and refines a temple and offers it to Shaligrama. Vatsaraja follows, Shambhudatta's son Bindupala, his son Rajapala, Bhumipala and Rangapala. Kalpasimha is the son of the best king Rangapala. Once he goes joyfully to the Ganga to bathe. The city named Kalapanagara is famous. A king at ninety years goes to war without a son. The remaining warriors of his line then all live as merchants and are like foreigners on earth.

08-002.json.summary: Suta tells of the lines of kings, each ruling like his father or for a number of years. Lakshmi (Rama) of Aja and Brahma is mentioned. Tomara, ruled ten years, is given Indraprastha by a pleased Shiva. Tomara's younger brother and a fine son of Chauhan follow. Mahadeva reigns seven years. Virasimha, Manikya, Chandragupta, Mohana, Nagavaha, Virasimha again, Chandraraya (fifty years), Vasanta, Pramatha, Vishala and Mantradeva follow, each ruling as his father did. Mantradeva conquers all Aryan lands. Anandadeva, a handsome son, is born, and his son rules like his father. Anangapala's sons are named: the eldest Dhundhukara at Mathura, the middle one, and the third, Mahiraja, strong, lord of Delhi. The chapter says Mahiraja went to heaven after casting shade on the Chauhan line. The women taken by foreigners became of mixed castes, and the Mehanas are of foreign birth, and the Jatts are called Aryan.

08-003.json.summary: Suta tells that Hari went to lovely Vrindavana on earth, and after sixty-eight thousand years Kali arrived in India with a foreign woman. Four thousand four hundred years are mentioned. Aryavati, the divine power, gladly took his tax. When the seven cities were destroyed, Brahmavarta was the best. Shukla reaches Raivata and goes to Mount Abu through the fire gate. Jayasena rules twenty years. Visena gives the kingdom to his son. Shripati is a son of the Gautama line. Bhujadesha becomes famous on earth. Dharmavarman, son of one who ruled like his father, builds a city for duty. Kalabhoja is his son. A pleased goddess has a city built. A girl, the goddess in bodily form, plays the flute, and a horse is given to someone. The king of birds Arkana is named in the east. Jayapala rules ten years. Govardhani and Sindura are called Kali. Chandradeva, the son, rules like his father. His lord, Mahamoda, follows the way of foreigners and ghouls. A wise man bows to Mahamoda. After conquering many kings at Kanyakubja, the line of Vaishyapala ends. The Gauhila Kshatriyas come from the line of Guhila. When Lakshana, the pillar of Shukla's line, dies, the rest are small kings of mixed castes.

08-004.json.summary: Suta continues the list of kings. A king meditates on the all-pervading eternal Shakti and is full of love. A place named Kalinjara becomes famous on earth. Gauravarman, his son, rules like his father and goes to the Gauda country to rule there. A king named Shaka worships the eternal Mahalakshmi and holds a great festival of Mahakali. A city named Kalikata becomes famous from the flower-buds she made gladly. Shivavarman, Rudravarman, Sukhasena, Lakshmana, Narayana and others follow, each ruling as his father did, and Narayana builds Shantipura on the Ganga bank. Nadivarman, Sharngadeva, Gangadeva, Narasimha and Dhritivarman follow. The chapter says all the Kshatriyas of the moon line were killed at Kurukshetra. Sahoddina rules twenty years. Ghoravarman is named, who by Mahamaya's grace was everywhere on earth. The last verse says the family destroys all sin, as the moon and sun do.

08-005.json.summary: Suta describes a time of dissolution at the end of a Manu's age. Mount Meru shakes again and again, the earth trembles, the seven continents and oceans become water, and the rest of the earth is dissolved. Vishnu, with Shiva and Brahma, takes all the stars and planets, and the circle of lights dries up all the earth. Brahma then makes the moon from his mouth, the strong king of warriors from his arms, the king of merchants and the ocean from his thighs, and the best craftsman Vishvakarma from his feet. Brahmins are born from the moon and the royal line from the sun. Vaivasvata Manu is born from the sun's disc. Vishnu is born from the first half and Vamana from the second. In the Kali age, Hari of the universal form himself dies. In the Satya age Hari is white and called Hamsa. In the Dvapara twilight the gods go to Vasudeva's house at Mathura, and the Lord tells them of Vrindavana, where in the dreadful Kali age all the Vedas become cowherd women. At the end of the Kali age, begged by Radha, he will end the age and become two bodies again. Hearing this, the gods vanish there. Vishnu devotees know the all-pervading one. The chapter ends with salutations to Mahakali, Vishnu's illusion, who made the whole moving and unmoving world of time.

08-006.json.summary: A sage and Suta speak of Bhupasena, grandson of Virasena. Hearing this, Sahoddina returns to Delhi. Vyasa tells the sages that the foreign kings will come, and they should go with him, all meditating in trance on Hari, the all-pervading. Manu speaks: the Supreme Brahman has looked on him, unlucky, with grace, and he asks what Suta and others did. Vyasa says the soul in this body is bound by the qualities of God, and that Narayana as the soul is deluded by Shankara. The kalpas Vayu, Agni, Brahmanda, Linga, Vamana, Narasimha, Varaha, Matsya and Kurma are named, with the Kurma first and Matsya second. He gives the number of human years: nineteen thousand and one lakh. The senses, mind and intellect are called attributes of the unmanifest, and the subtle mind, joined to breath, goes to Brahma's place. All the holy places and the Vedas leave the earth. A king, a form of time, conquers the Aryan and foreign kings, and a king builds a fort in the Taittira land. The gods say they are all in the Shaligrama stones. The king of gods tells Mahendra with the gods something worthy of worship. Jiva (Brihaspati) says the goddess has by his order made a peaceful city. The sages with the eleven Rudras go to Prayaga, king of holy places, dear to the sun, and Brihaspati comes and tells the best greatness of the sun.

08-007.json.summary: The sages ask Brihaspati to tell the best greatness of the sun. A Brahmin Dhatrisharma asks Prajapati for a child, has three children after a year, and is pleased with his daughter-in-law and son-in-law. The Lord pleases him with much wealth. In his fifth year the sun, kind to devotees, speaks of a subtle divine light in the unmanifest. A dark deluding mind is told of, whose husband is Shiva himself. Union is gained through knowledge. Suta says that the Brahmin Dhatrisharma reached liberation in the sun. Brihaspati tells how Mitrasharma, after getting the daughter of Kamasena, returns home, and a woman of picture-like beauty worships the sun. He recites the Aditya hridaya hymn, devoted to the sun. The two choose Mitrasharma and ask for his daughter. Both, in bodies of a hundred years, are ageless and free of tiredness. A Brahmin, thinking it over, uses the power of the jewel to get a measure of gold. Brihaspati tells that a person known as Nimbaditya will remove the decline of duty, and says that a child is born to Jayanti, a faithful wife, in a form of victory. When the sun reaches the setting mountain, a boy in a beggar's dress, like a second sun, is honoured with "well done".

08-008.json.summary: Brihaspati tells the story of the Ashvins, Rudras, Vasus and Suryas separately, and a ruling post held for a hundred thousand years in the sun's disc. A son of the Brahmin Madhava is foretold. A farmer who gives a tenth of his income is named. A king is distressed and calls Megharsharma, who is told to have the rite done properly and be happy. A garden is given to a man: "this is my lovely garden, go there and be happy". Pranshusharma is very sad in the morning when the sun arrives. Vishnusharma, son of Shivadatta, is told of. Vishnusvami comes to be. A goddess appears, pleased at his austerity. A revived person is shown and the others are amazed. A woman named Sushila comes to serve her husband. A Brahmin has faith in the sun daily. The sun tells Indra "I do the gods' work". After three years the Lord gives great knowledge to someone. A bull is called Nandiyana. A blacksmith and poverty in the form of iron are mentioned. A line says wealth without duty never shines. A son is said to go to the sea, guarded by Rakshasis. The king bows to the best Vaishnava Brahmin. The Vedanga and the course of the stars were destroyed by foreigners.

08-009.json.summary: Suta says that after Jiva told the greatness of the sun, the sun was born at Pratishthanapura by Shiva's command. At the end of the Treta age there was King Parikshit in Sri Lanka. A maiden bows her neck to a sage who speaks of the nine doors of the body always full of bad smells. Shiva, seeing the sage turned leper, speaks to him. The Lord tells the gods something. The sun goes to Kashi. The body wasted by diseases is called a "kalpa" by the wise, and Sushruta's Kalpaveda made by Dhanvantari is named, with the arts of metals and all crafts. The sun is satisfied by many sacrifices and eats every day. The sun goes to Vanga. Parents who died are satisfied with rites for the dead. In the twenty-third year a sweet-faced woman tells Satyavrata that Jayadeva is his own body. He composes the Vedic Nirukta, and five kinds of Nirukta are named. Kali, the wily one in the heart of thieves, appears once. The goddess, sorrowful, sees her husband in a pit. King Dharmapala hears and is amazed, and speaks to Jayadeva. The learned say they came to his house skilled in scriptures. A Brahmin of Gauda country, who was our pupil, was woken by us. When the Brahmin weeps, his hands and feet return to their natural state. The king is pleased with Jayadeva's words. This is how Jayadeva came to be.

08-010.json.summary: Jiva (Brihaspati) speaks. Someone becomes worshipped by other gods through worship of Hari. A touchstone turns iron into gold. A man says he is devoted to Vishnu, poor and afraid of thieves, and a Brahmin throws the wealth by force into a deep jar. A beggar is deluded by fate. An ascetic bows to a Brahmin and speaks humbly. In the month of Phalguna the Brahmin takes up Vaishnava light. Jiva speaks to Indra again. The god, after the guru's instruction, meditates on Hari, the all-pervading. Two, joined together, are tormented by Vishnu's fire. Rudras, Vasus, Vishvedevas and Maruts appear. A hymn is addressed to Shachinandana, who brings joy, removes the heat of great sin and appears in the Kali age to give the unfamiliar. The earth is distressed by the enemies of the gods and unjust persons. Brihaspati says Brahmins make a mistake by taking a Shudra's property as blood. Brahma, grieved, tells the seven sages. Marichi and others laugh and ask why he wants to kill. The sages leave for different holy places. Valmiki is called so because he came out of an anthill. A deer-hunter, the eternal lord, still stands. From the arms came the Kshatriya, from the thighs the Vaishya. Kashyapa is the second and Marichi came after. Various creations arose in the Vaivasvata period. Shiva, angry as a hunter, became Virabhadra. Rudra is glad. A boy becomes virtuous, wise and a student, with the tripundra, rosary and five-syllable mantra.
